# 1 August: Toward the Switzerland of Tomorrow

> On Swiss National Day we look back to a pact from 1291 — and forward. What Switzerland's founding idea means for the next hundred years.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/aktuelles/1-august-2026/ · Published: 2026-08-01 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

1 August commemorates a federal charter from 1291. 735 years on, we are not celebrating a museum piece but an idea that has stayed remarkably modern: that people shape their future better together and self-determined than alone and governed from outside.

---

## A founding act that faced forward

1291 was not a look backward. It was a decision to reorder how people lived together, to create legal certainty, and to withstand outside pressure jointly. Switzerland was not born of nostalgia but of a pragmatic need for stability and self-determination.

It is precisely that instinct — solving problems soberly, building institutions that last, choosing reliability over loud gestures — that has carried the country through seven centuries. It is not an heirloom to put on a shelf. It is a way of working.

---

## The substance is built today

The coming decades bring shifts that reach deeper than any single term of office: artificial intelligence, energy, demographics, the new order of the world economy. The question is not whether Switzerland will change. The question is whether it shapes that change itself — sovereign, resilient, clear-eyed — or lets it happen to it.

What we build or neglect over the next ten years will decide how free and prosperous Switzerland is in 2050. That substance appears in no ranking. It is being built now.

---

## A holiday is also a charge

On 1 August we rightly celebrate what the generations before us built: a country that works, that holds its diversity together, that enjoys trust beyond its size. To preserve that inheritance is not to freeze it. It is to keep building it.

The best way to honor Switzerland is to keep it fit for the future.

---

We wish everyone a wonderful National Day — and we invite you to help build the Switzerland of tomorrow with us.

[Our programme](@/programm.en.md) · [Get involved](@/mitmachen.en.md)

---

# 14 June 2026 vote: two proposals, three pillars

> On 14 June, Switzerland votes on the 10-million initiative and the amendment to the Civilian Service Act. A reading along the programme of The Future.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/aktuelles/abstimmung-14-juni-2026/ · Published: 2026-06-03 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

On 14 June 2026 Switzerland votes on two federal proposals: the popular initiative "No to a Switzerland with 10 million! (Sustainability Initiative)" and the amendment to the Civilian Service Act. Both touch questions we have worked on from the start — how to attract talent, how to keep cities and infrastructure sustainable, how to build civil and military readiness at the same time. We do not issue a voting recommendation here. We show where the two proposals meet our programme, and where, from our perspective, the honest tensions lie.

**Update (result).** Both proposals have been decided: the popular initiative "No to a Switzerland with 10 million!" was rejected with 54.8% no, and the amendment to the Civilian Service Act was accepted with 53.0% yes (turnout 58.9%). The framing below was written before voting Sunday and stands unchanged as a programme reading.

---

## Proposal 1: "No to a Switzerland with 10 million!"

The SVP initiative wants to cap Switzerland's permanent resident population at ten million people by 2050. If that threshold were crossed earlier, the Federal Council would have to renegotiate or terminate the free movement of persons agreements with the EU. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend rejection.

Our programme reads this proposal along two pillars.

**Talent & integration.** Switzerland owes its prosperity to its ability to attract researchers, engineers, care workers and founders. A rigid cap is a blunt tool: it does not distinguish between unmanaged growth and the targeted inflow of specialists who will carry the next twenty years. Talent pathways need to be shorter, not longer.

**Cities & housing.** The other half of the truth: infrastructure — housing, public transport, schools, hospitals, energy — has for years grown more slowly than the population. Whoever wants inflow must also build, plan, train. The initiative responds to a real failure, but with a quantity cap rather than with construction and planning capacity.

The question behind the proposal is therefore not "how many people" but "how much substance do we build so that Switzerland can carry the people it needs". A ceiling without a plan solves none of the underlying problems.

---

## Proposal 2: amendment to the Civilian Service Act

Parliament revised the Civilian Service Act, a referendum brought the proposal before the people. Six measures are intended to make admission to civilian service harder, so that the constitutional rule — no free choice between army and civilian service — is enforced more strictly. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend acceptance.

Our programme reads this proposal along one pillar.

**Neutrality & peace.** Switzerland needs both: a credible army and a civil resilience that absorbs crises — blackouts, pandemics, cyberattacks, climate events. People in civilian service work in hospitals, in agriculture, in nature conservation, in schools. They are not a residual position but part of a country's civil readiness.

The tension in this proposal is real and honest: every person who switches to civilian service is missing from the army. But every person who cannot enter civilian service is missing from civil supply. The question is whether Switzerland should solve a shortage in one place by creating a shortage in another — or whether both pillars need to be strengthened at the same time.

By the logic of our programme, this is not a pure army question. It is a question of how we understand resilience as a whole.

---

## How we frame it

Both proposals address real Swiss problems — infrastructure pressure and security architecture — with tools we consider too narrow. A population cap is not a housing policy. An admission hurdle is not a civil protection strategy.

Our contribution is not to tell the population where to put the cross. Our contribution is to describe the long-term substance against which Switzerland will be measured over the next twenty years. We have summarized it in our [programme](@/programm.en.md) as twelve pillars. The two proposals on 14 June touch three of them. Whoever votes can take this reading as one voice among many.

---

## About the tracker

We are building a permanent overview of federal popular votes at [/en/abstimmungen/](@/abstimmungen.en.md). For each voting Sunday it carries a brief framing per proposal along our pillars — no voting recommendation, but a clear programme perspective. Next dates: 27 September 2026, 29 November 2026.

Sources: [Federal Chancellery — 14 June 2026](https://www.admin.ch/en/popular-vote-of-14-june-2026), [ch.ch — Popular vote 14 June 2026](https://www.ch.ch/en/votes-and-elections/popular-vote-on-14-june-2026/), [EAER on the Civilian Service Act amendment](https://www.wbf.admin.ch/de/newnsb/NqqjJZsMpWsniYOTjgfl8), [Federal Council on the civilian service amendment](https://www.admin.ch/de/aenderung-zivildienst), [easyvote](https://www.easyvote.ch/de/abstimmungen/14-juni-2026/zivildienstgesetz).

---

# 27 September 2026 vote: two initiatives, three pillars

> On 27 September, Switzerland votes on the Neutrality Initiative and the Nutrition Initiative. A reading along the programme of The Future.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/aktuelles/abstimmung-27-september-2026/ · Published: 2026-09-16 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

On 27 September 2026 Switzerland votes on two popular initiatives: "Preserving Swiss neutrality (Neutrality Initiative)" and "For secure nutrition (Nutrition Initiative)". Both want to write something into the constitution that is meant to make Switzerland more independent — one in foreign policy, the other in supply. Both touch questions we have worked on from the start: what neutrality has to deliver today, how a country becomes resilient, how progress and trust go together. We do not issue a voting recommendation here. We show where the two initiatives meet our programme, and where, from our perspective, the honest tensions lie.

**Update (result).** On 27 September 2026 voters rejected both initiatives: the Neutrality Initiative with 70.2% no, the Nutrition Initiative with 72.5% no. Both were also rejected by every canton (turnout around 47%). The framing below was written before voting Sunday and stands unchanged as a programme reading.

---

## Proposal 1: Neutrality Initiative

The initiative, launched from the SVP's orbit, wants to spell neutrality out in detail in the Federal Constitution: perpetual and armed. Switzerland could neither join a military or defence alliance nor cooperate with one — unless it is attacked or an attack is being prepared. Economic sanctions against warring states would be permitted only if decided by the UN Security Council; measures against the circumvention of foreign sanctions would remain possible. At the same time, Switzerland is to use its neutrality actively for conflict prevention and mediation. The initiative was launched after Switzerland adopted the EU sanctions against Russia in 2022. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend rejection; the National Council rejected it 124 to 65, the Council of States 29 to 10. There is no counter-proposal.

Our programme reads this proposal along two pillars.

**Neutrality & peace.** Much of what the initiative demands is, in substance, in our programme: no participation in wars between states, no offensive military adventures, active peace work — mediating, hosting, helping on humanitarian grounds. For us, neutrality is not a myth but a strategic asset: it makes Switzerland the place where parties to a conflict still talk to each other. The question is not whether Switzerland stays neutral. The question is whether a detailed constitutional article strengthens that credibility — or whether credibility is earned day by day through practice, consistency and trust. The sanctions clause is the core of the tension: the UN Security Council is often blocked by vetoes. Switzerland would therefore have to forgo economic measures in most of the wars of our time — and defend the international law on which a small neutral state relies by other means.

**Energy & infrastructure resilience.** The threats have changed: hybrid risks, sabotage, cyberattacks, failures of critical infrastructure. Our programme says: build protective capability without becoming aggressive — and cooperate with European partners where that raises resilience. The alliance ban is the second tension here. The initiative allows training with foreign partners and peace missions approved by Parliament. But defence against sabotage and cyberattacks begins long before an armed attack. Whether the cooperation a strictly defensive Switzerland needs for that would still be possible under a ban on cooperation is left open by the proposal.

So the question behind the proposal is not "neutral or not". It is: how much neutrality do you write into paragraphs — and how much must a country earn anew every day through credible conduct?

---

## Proposal 2: Nutrition Initiative

The initiative demands that Switzerland reach a net self-sufficiency rate of at least 70 percent within ten years. To get there, the Confederation is to strengthen sustainable domestic production, promote more plant-based and fewer animal foods, protect soil fertility and biodiversity, cut the use of pesticides and fertilisers, and secure clean drinking water. Today the net self-sufficiency rate — that is, after deducting imported animal feed — stands at around 42 to 45 percent and is falling. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend rejection; both chambers rejected the initiative without a single dissenting vote (194 to 0 in the National Council, 44 to 0 in the Council of States). They consider the target unreachable within ten years and expect high costs and heavy intervention in production and consumption.

Our programme reads this proposal along two pillars.

**Energy & infrastructure resilience.** Food is supply, and supply is infrastructure. The initiative names a real dependence: less than half of what Switzerland eats is, in net terms, produced at home. Our programme takes such dependences seriously — pragmatically and risk-based. For us, resilience is engineering: standards, redundancy, stockpiling, accountability. A percentage in the constitution is a target, not a plan. The tension is that the initiative sets the target but leaves open how Switzerland produces substantially more with the same land and fewer inputs. That takes precision agriculture, robotics, breeding, water planning — substance that cannot be ordered by a vote but has to be built.

**Life science & health.** More plant-based nutrition and clean drinking water are health questions, and the direction is well documented. But our yardstick remains: regulation that is evidence-based and transparent, progress with trust. A rigid ten-year target that would have to be enforced through production and consumption rules moves the decision from the plate to the ordinance. Switzerland is a world leader in the life sciences — that knowledge belongs in agriculture, not only in the pharmaceutical industry.

So the question behind the proposal is not "how many percent". It is: how does Switzerland build a supply that survives a crisis — and who carries the cost of the transition?

---

## How we frame this

Both initiatives respond to the same experience: Switzerland is more dependent than it feels — on foreign alliances and sanctions regimes, on imported food and feed. We share that diagnosis. Both initiatives answer with a constitutional sentence: a fixed rule that prescribes independence. That, in our view, is where the limit lies. Neutrality does not become more credible because it is worded at greater length. Supply does not become more secure because a number stands in the constitution. Both come from substance: protective capability, mediation competence, stockpiling, technology, reliability.

Our contribution is not to tell people where to put the cross. Our contribution is to describe the long-term substance by which Switzerland will be measured over the next twenty years. We have summarised it in our [programme](@/programm.en.md) as twelve pillars. The two initiatives on 27 September touch three of them. Whoever votes can take this reading as one voice among many.

---

## About the tracker

At [/en/abstimmungen/](@/abstimmungen.en.md) we keep a permanent overview of federal popular votes: for each voting Sunday a brief framing per proposal along our pillars — no voting recommendation, but a clear programme perspective. Next date after 27 September: 29 November 2026.

Sources: [Federal Chancellery — 27 September 2026](https://www.admin.ch/de/volksabstimmung-vom-27-september-2026), [Federal Council on the Neutrality Initiative](https://www.admin.ch/de/neutralitaetsinitiative), [Federal Council on the Nutrition Initiative](https://www.admin.ch/de/ernaehrungsinitiative), [ch.ch — Popular vote 27 September 2026](https://www.ch.ch/de/volksabstimmung-vom-27-september-2026/), [easyvote — Neutrality Initiative](https://www.easyvote.ch/de/abstimmungen/27-september-2026/neutralitaet), [easyvote — Nutrition Initiative](https://www.easyvote.ch/de/abstimmungen/27-september-2026/ernaehrung).

---

# 29 November 2026 vote: four proposals, five pillars

> On 29 November, Switzerland votes on additional AHV financing, the fireworks initiative, the married-couples initiative and the War Material Act. A reading along the programme of The Future.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/aktuelles/abstimmung-29-november-2026/ · Published: 2026-09-18 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

On 29 November 2026 Switzerland votes on four federal proposals: the federal decree on additional financing of the AHV old-age pension through VAT, the popular initiative "For a restriction of fireworks", the popular initiative "Yes to fair federal taxes for married couples too – end the discrimination of marriage!", and the amendment to the War Material Act. Four very different topics — and yet one shared question: at what level, and with what instrument, does Switzerland take its decisions? We do not issue a voting recommendation here. We show where the four proposals meet our programme, and where, from our perspective, the honest tensions lie. This framing was written on the basis of Parliament's decisions, before the Federal Council's official explanations were published.

**Update of 20 October 2026.** We checked this framing against the Federal Council's official explanations (the voting booklet) and corrected facts: the VAT increase brings the AHV around CHF 1.4 billion a year, not 1.5 billion, and together with the federal contribution covers about half of the additional cost of the 13th AHV pension (previously: about a third). The Federal Council puts the possible revenue losses from the married-couples initiative at CHF 680 million to 3 billion a year (previously: 700 million to 1.4 billion); in Parliament the votes were 102 to 97 in the National Council and 24 to 20 in the Council of States. For the War Material Act we added the relaxations for partner states and for non-re-export declarations; for the fireworks initiative we clarified what would remain allowed. Our programme reading stands unchanged.

---

## Proposal 1: additional AHV financing through VAT

In March 2024 voters accepted the 13th AHV pension. It is paid for the first time in December 2026 to around 2.6 million pensioners and costs over CHF 4 billion at first, over 5 billion a year from 2035. On 19 June 2026 Parliament decided to fund it by raising VAT by 0.4 percentage points, without time limit and from 2028 at the earliest: the standard rate from 8.1 to 8.5 percent, the special rate for accommodation from 3.8 to 4 percent; the reduced rate for food and medicines stays at 2.6 percent. That brings the AHV around CHF 1.4 billion a year from 2029; the payments in 2026 and 2027 have no additional financing. Higher wage contributions, which were also on the table, were dropped by Parliament. Because VAT is anchored in the constitution, the vote is mandatory and needs a double majority of people and cantons. The National Council approved 108 to 85, the Council of States 28 to 13. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend acceptance.

Our programme reads this proposal along two pillars.

**Basic income.** For us, a universal basic security is a foundation, not a gift — and it has to be financed by taxing growing value creation: income, consumption, wealth. Not through wages alone, when an ever larger share of value comes from automation. VAT as the lever for a pension everyone receives sits within that logic; the same lever is built into our basic-income calculator. Mechanically, the proposal is close to what we describe for a basic income.

**Open government.** The tension lies in the honesty of the arithmetic. Together with the federal contribution, the 1.4 billion covers about half of the additional cost; the rest stays open and weighs on the AHV fund, whose spending already exceeds its revenue in 2026. Transparent budgets are not a detail for us but a standard: a benefit promise that is half unfunded is a stopgap. Whoever votes yes funds a part. Whoever votes no funds nothing for now — the pension is paid regardless.

So the question behind the proposal is not "VAT or not". It is: when does Switzerland put the full bill for the 13th pension on the table — and on what base is it paid in an automated economy?

---

## Proposal 2: fireworks initiative

The initiative by four animal-welfare organisations wants a nationwide ban on the sale and use of loud fireworks by private individuals. The text leaves open which fireworks count as noise-producing; according to the initiative committee, low-noise fireworks such as Bengal lights or fountains would remain allowed. For events of supra-regional importance, cantons could grant exceptions. More than a hundred municipalities already have restrictions. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend rejection (National Council 131 to 50, Council of States 40 to 3), with no counter-proposal: cantons and municipalities can already limit fireworks in time and place. An indirect counter-proposal that would have banned only noise-only firecrackers in the Explosives Act failed in the National Council's final vote on 19 June 2026, 114 to 79. So the initiative goes to the people unchanged.

Our programme reads this proposal along one pillar.

**Cities & housing.** We want cities to grow inward: denser, closer, with short distances. But density also means more people, pets and wildlife live within earshot of the same fireworks. In a densified Switzerland, consideration is not a matter of taste but part of quality of life. So the initiative names a real problem. The tension lies in the instrument and the level: a constitutional article for a question every municipality can settle for itself today — and more than a hundred already do. On the other hand, Parliament itself discarded every milder national rule. Whoever votes no relies on local rules. Whoever votes yes lifts the rule from the municipalities into the constitution.

So the question behind the proposal is not "fireworks yes or no". It is: at what level does Switzerland organise consideration — and what happens when the local level does not?

---

## Proposal 3: married-couples initiative

The Centre party's popular initiative wants to abolish the marriage penalty in direct federal tax through the constitution. Married couples would continue to be assessed jointly but could no longer be disadvantaged compared with unmarried couples. On 8 March 2026 voters accepted individual taxation with 54 percent, which solves the same problem with the opposite model: each person is taxed separately, regardless of civil status. The initiative would again prescribe a different system for federal tax. Depending on implementation, the Federal Council expects direct federal tax revenue losses of CHF 680 million to 3 billion a year. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend rejection — the National Council 102 to 97, the Council of States 24 to 20.

Our programme reads this proposal along one pillar.

**Open government.** A state that enables rather than blocks has simple, transparent procedures. We share the initiative's goal — no disadvantage based on civil status. But that is exactly the goal Switzerland already decided in March. The tension is that the initiative does not decide the whether but the how: joint assessment at the federal level while the cantons switch to individual taxation — two logics for the same people. That costs revenue and simplicity. Whoever votes yes chooses the joint-assessment model and accepts the duplication. Whoever votes no lets the individual taxation decided in March take effect.

So the question behind the proposal is not "abolish the marriage penalty or not" — that is settled. It is: which model should apply, and how many parallel systems can a simple state bear?

---

## Proposal 4: amendment to the War Material Act

In December 2025 Parliament decided to relax the rules for exporting and re-exporting war material. Three points are central: the 36 partner states with export controls similar to Switzerland's can be supplied even when involved in an armed conflict, provided neutrality law and foreign or security policy interests do not stand in the way. The Federal Council will require non-re-export declarations only where foreign, neutrality or security policy reasons demand it. And the Federal Council can deviate from the statutory licensing criteria in extraordinary circumstances to safeguard Switzerland's foreign or security policy interests; if it does so by ordinance, the ordinance is limited to four years at most, and it must inform Parliament's security policy committees within 24 hours of an individual decision. In 2021 Parliament had written those criteria firmly into law — no exports to countries in armed conflict, for example — and declined such an exception clause; the "correction initiative" was withdrawn as a result. Now the clause returns, justified by the situation since 2022 and the concerns of the Swiss security industry. The National Council approved 122 to 68, the Council of States 31 to 11. A referendum by the SP, the Greens, the EVP, the GSoA and aid organisations brings the proposal to the people. The Federal Council and Parliament recommend acceptance.

Our programme reads this proposal along two pillars.

**Neutrality & peace.** Our guardrails are clear: strictly defensive, neutral and credible, transparent and bound by the rule of law — clear mandates, clear responsibilities, democratic control. The tension sits exactly there: the proposal moves a decision that the law takes today into the Federal Council's discretion. In a crisis that can be faster. But it makes Swiss practice harder to predict — and predictability is the capital of a neutral country that wants to mediate.

**Energy & infrastructure resilience.** The other side: protective capability needs an industrial base. Whoever wants to reduce critical dependences in components, spare parts and know-how needs firms that produce in the country — and they only do so if they can also export and cooperate with European partners. Since 2022, firms report that partners avoid Swiss components. That concern is real. Whether the answer is a discretionary clause for the executive or clearer rules set by Parliament is the actual question.

So the question behind the proposal is not "arms exports yes or no". It is: how much flexibility does Switzerland need — and who answers for it: the law or the Federal Council?

---

## How we frame this

Four proposals, four topics — and one shared pattern: each moves a decision to a different level. The fireworks initiative lifts a municipal rule into the constitution. The married-couples initiative places a second model next to a law just adopted. The War Material Act shifts a statutory rule into the Federal Council's discretion. And the AHV proposal funds part of a promise whose remainder stays open.

Our yardstick is the same in all four cases: a rule must be clear, financed, democratically controllable — and located where it works best. That is not a question of left or right. It is the question of whether the state stays simple, honest and reliable.

Our contribution is not to tell people where to put the cross. Our contribution is to describe the long-term substance by which Switzerland will be measured over the next twenty years. We have summarised it in our [programme](@/programm.en.md) as twelve pillars. The four proposals on 29 November touch five of them. Whoever votes can take this reading as one voice among many.

---

## About the tracker

At [/en/abstimmungen/](@/abstimmungen.en.md) we keep a permanent overview of federal popular votes: for each voting Sunday a brief framing per proposal along our pillars — no voting recommendation, but a clear programme perspective. The framing for 27 September 2026 is in the article [27 September 2026 vote: two initiatives, three pillars](@/aktuelles/abstimmung-27-september-2026.en.md). On 20 October 2026 we checked this article against the Federal Council's explanations (see the update at the top).

Sources: [Federal Chancellery: popular vote of 29 November 2026](https://www.admin.ch/de/volksabstimmung-vom-29-november-2026), [Federal Council explanations for 29 November 2026 (PDF)](https://www.admin.ch/dam/de/sd-web/HXhFMFWOaa6u/BAR_Erlaeuterungen_Nov26_DE_v10.pdf), [Federal Council: ballot items for 29 November 2026](https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/KpnrPOW9cpZAvB6IXOekf), [Parliament: VAT raised for the 13th AHV pension](https://www.parlament.ch/de/services/news/Seiten/2026/20260619094409246194158159026_bsd047.aspx), [FSIO: implementing the 13th AHV pension](https://www.bsv.admin.ch/de/umsetzung-13-ahv-rente), [Parliament: National Council sinks national firecracker ban](https://www.parlament.ch/de/services/news/Seiten/2026/20260619160127130194158159026_bsd140.aspx), [swissinfo: Council of States says no to the Centre initiative](https://www.swissinfo.ch/ger/st%C3%A4nderat-sagt-nein-zur-mitte-initiative-gegen-die-heiratsstrafe/91526866), [Federal Chancellery: referendum on the War Material Act](https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/6FKPS4DauZHEk2eUaf-eO), [Swissvotes: amendment to the War Material Act](https://swissvotes.ch/vote/693.00).

# The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It

> The AI debate is about compute. The real bottleneck is high-quality, rights-clear data — and Europe holds more of it than anyone. Using it is a question of coordination.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/aktuelles/der-engpass-sind-die-daten/ · Published: 2026-06-30 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

The public debate about who leads in artificial intelligence is almost entirely a debate about hardware. Who has the most accelerators, who controls the fabs, whose export controls bite whose supply chain. That debate is real. It is also, increasingly, looking in the wrong place.

The people running the largest AI labs say so themselves. In late 2024, Ilya Sutskever said that pre-training "as we know it" would end — for the blunt reason that compute keeps growing but data does not, "because we have but one internet." He called data "the fossil fuel of AI." If the scarce input is high-quality data, then the real question becomes: who holds the data that has not yet been consumed? The answer, for a large and very specific category, is Europe.

---

## The raw material is running short

The most careful public estimate comes from Epoch AI: roughly 300 trillion tokens of publicly available, human-generated text, fully used up at some point between 2026 and 2032. That is not a prediction of a wall. It is a prediction that the easy phase is ending — the one where you gained capability mostly by pointing a larger crawler at a larger share of the same web.

The raw web is vast, but most of it is not worth training on. Between petabytes of HTML and a few tens of trillions of clean tokens is the whole game. Quantity was never the bottleneck. Clean, relevant, rights-clear quantity is.

How scarce that raw material has become is shown by the behaviour of the largest labs. They took legal and reputational risk to get more text — up to billion-dollar settlements and the use of shadow libraries. When a company with practically unlimited access to the open web takes that kind of risk, the text has become the scarce input.

---

## What Europe — and Switzerland — hold

This is where the map flips. The text the crawlers cannot reach, because it was never digitized or never made public, is disproportionately European — and disproportionately the high-quality kind. Europe printed, archived, and catalogued for five centuries, across two dozen living languages, and for the most part never put the result on the open web.

The cleanest example is in Zurich. The Neue Zürcher Zeitung digitized its entire print run back to its first edition in 1780, around 1.9 million pages. It is one of the most complete continuous records of European public life in machine-readable form. Yet free access stops at 1914. Everything after — that is, exactly the century that shaped modern Europe — is reserved for paying customers. That is one newspaper, in one city, in one of the smaller countries of Europe. Multiply that pattern across every national paper, every learned society, every specialist journal on the continent, and the size of the locked corpus comes into view.

That clean training data can be made from it is not hypothetical. In 2025 Harvard Library released, from its digitized collections, a 242-billion-token dataset with traceable provenance. A single university library. The European version of that move, carried out across the continent's libraries and archives, would yield a corpus with no equivalent anywhere else.

There is a second advantage the incumbents structurally cannot replicate: aligned multilingual text. The EU works in 24 official languages; decades of parliamentary and legal translation have produced parallel corpora that exist for almost no other language in the world. Switzerland, with its four national languages, knows this asset from its own administration. For the long tail of underrepresented European languages, this text is exactly what makes the difference between a usable model and a useless one.

---

## A coordination problem, not a technology problem

Why does this advantage lie fallow? Because it is fragmented, and the fragmentation is structural. A French library, a Swiss newspaper, a German learned society, an Italian state archive each hold a piece, each under a different legal regime, none with the mandate or budget to turn its holdings into training data. The technical problem has been solved for years. The hard problem is institutional, legal, and political.

The legal situation is double-edged. Europe has built the densest data-governance apparatus in the world — and so far protection has outrun enablement. But the tools are there. The 2019 copyright directive grants research organizations and cultural-heritage institutions a mandatory, non-waivable exception for text and data mining, on any work to which they have lawful access. And it is precisely those institutions that hold the locked corpus. It is the most underused lever in European AI policy.

---

## It is already starting

The proof of concept is done, by small teams on modest budgets. Common Corpus, assembled by the French company PleIAs, is at roughly 2.3 trillion tokens the largest fully open multilingual training corpus — built only from public-domain and openly licensed material, with per-document provenance. Alongside it, sovereign models have appeared in two years: Teuken from Germany, EuroLLM, Spain's ALIA, Latvia's TildeOpen, plus an open European web index. Read individually, these are regional projects. Read together, they are a continent rediscovering the same insight from a dozen directions. What is missing is the layer above them: a shared corpus, a coordinated digitization programme, a budget that treats the data as strategic infrastructure rather than as a collection of national research grants.

---

## What this means for our programme

The Future has argued from the start for digital sovereignty through open standards, transparency, and anti-lock-in. The data bottleneck is the reason for that, not a slogan. Concretely:

- **Fund digitization as infrastructure, not as a cultural grant.** Libraries, archives, and newspaper morgues are, for the AI substrate, what roads and grid capacity are for the economy. They depreciate while they sit in boxes.
- **Use the mining exception with legal certainty.** Route digitization and corpus-building through the institutions that hold the lawful access.
- **Keep the corpus and the index open.** A shared open corpus means every lab competes on models, not on data hoards. A proprietary corpus reproduces exactly the dependency the whole effort is meant to escape.
- **Bring Switzerland in.** Swiss libraries, archives, and the multilingual administrative record belong in the European data space — and tied to sovereign compute, operated under domestic law.

The goal is not to "win the AI race." That is the wrong frame. The realistic goal is sovereign capability: models that are better in our languages, trained on rights-clear data that survives an audit, and usable by regulated sectors that legally cannot run on a corpus of uncertain provenance. That is a niche the giants cannot easily contest — and it sits exactly where Europe's data advantage lies.

---

## Further reading

This note is the civilian translation of a sister article published today, 30 June 2026:

- *The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It* on [raskell.io](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bottleneck-is-data-and-europe-is-sitting-on-it/) (engineer's perspective, with full sources)

Sources: [Epoch AI on the data limit](https://epoch.ai/publications/will-we-run-out-of-data-limits-of-llm-scaling-based-on-human-generated-data), [DSM Directive 2019/790](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj), [Common Corpus (PleIAs)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PleIAs/common_corpus), [NZZ archive](https://zeitungsarchiv.nzz.ch/), [Harvard Institutional Books](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.08300).

# A new face – and why we build it in the open

> The Future has a new website: clearer in its message, deeper in its content, with a new brand. What has changed, how we decided and why we develop everything in public.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/aktuelles/neues-gesicht/ · Published: 2026-11-07 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

As of today, the new website of The Future is online. It looks different, but above all it says more clearly what we stand for: artificial intelligence and robotics can create prosperity for everyone. For that to happen, Switzerland needs a plan. The website should be able to show that plan in three seconds and explain it in three hours.

---

## First the stance, then the depth

The old website was a sequence of slides. You scrolled, a page snapped into place, the next one followed. It felt calm, but it hid two things: our message and the depth behind it.

The new homepage works in layers. At the very top is what we want: "The Future. We build it." and three phrases that sum up our stance: prosperity over scarcity thinking, security over fear, sovereignty over dependence. Below come the ten theses of the [manifesto](@/manifest.en.md), then all thirteen pillars of the [programme](@/programm.en.md) at a glance, then the evidence from the [Future Lab](@/zukunftslabor/_index.en.md). If you only have a minute, you will understand us. If you have an evening, you will find the sources.

![The new homepage: wordmark, core statement and the Swiss cross made of cubes in the background](https://die-zukunft.ch/aktuelles/neues-gesicht/startseite.webp)

---

## A tangible future instead of science fiction

The website was meant to feel futuristic, but not kitschy. No neon colours, no robot eyes. We took our cues from things you can touch: a light ground like ceramic, dark ink, fine lines as on a construction drawing. Behind every page stands the same object, a three-dimensional Swiss cross made of cubes. It turns slowly, responds to scrolling and steps back as soon as the text takes over.

The new colour is called **Alpenglühen** (alpenglow): pink, magenta, violet and indigo, like the mountains in the first light of day. It stands for optimism without pathos and is clearly distinct from the colours of the established parties.

The new icon, the **Würfelkreuz** (cube cross), is made of seven cubes. A Swiss cross assembled from building blocks: that is exactly what we intend to do in politics.

---

## How we decided

We did not decide at the drawing board, but by direct comparison. For the wordmark we put fifteen variants side by side, for the colour nine palettes, for the icon fourteen drafts, each one large and small, light and dark, in all four languages. Some things we tried and dropped again, such as a red full stop in the wordmark. What remained is what works just as well on a phone as on a poster.

![Nine colour palettes compared, here the chosen Alpenglühen](https://die-zukunft.ch/aktuelles/neues-gesicht/paletten.webp)

It is the same method we propose for politics: lay the options side by side, test them, decide, and document openly why.

---

## What is new

- **The vision as a blueprint.** The [vision](@/vision.en.md) shows "the abundance stack": from energy through compute, sovereign AI and talent to application in every sector and a dividend for everyone. With figures, sources and targets with dates attached.
- **A new pillar.** [Sovereign AI & Compute](@/souveraene-ki.en.md) now comes first in the programme, because everything else builds on it.
- **The manifesto, version 2.0.** Ten theses, each with a permanent address you can link to and quote.
- **Pinning.** You can pin any section and find it again later. The pins stay in your browser, with no account and no cookies, and can be shared as a link.
- **Calmer on your phone.** Many of you complained about the "magnetic" snapping while scrolling, especially on the iPhone. It is gone. The page scrolls freely, and forms no longer zoom in uninvited.

![The new website on the iPhone](https://die-zukunft.ch/aktuelles/neues-gesicht/iphone.webp)

---

## Built in the open

Every section has an address in the corner, for example 0x1002 for the first thesis. That gives away how we work: like an open software project. The website's source code, the design and all brand assets are public on [GitHub](https://github.com/zukunft-ch). At the bottom of every page you can see how much it weighs, measured in your browser, and that it runs without trackers.

If you find a mistake, have a better wording or want to improve a translation, you can contribute directly, with an issue or a pull request. A party that calls for open government should work openly itself.

The future is a construction project. So is this website. [Build it with us.](@/mitmachen.en.md)

---

# Switzerland Is Number One. That Should Worry Us.

> Switzerland tops the Global Innovation Index for the fifteenth year running. That describes the past. The substance we will be measured on is being built today.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/aktuelles/platz-1-ist-kein-plan/ · Published: 2026-05-01 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Switzerland tops the Global Innovation Index for the fifteenth consecutive year. 66.0 out of 100, ahead of Sweden, the United States, Korea, and Singapore. It is a remarkable result. It is also a description of the past.

Rankings measure outputs. Outputs come from decisions made ten to fifteen years earlier. What we see today on the index is the harvest of the Swiss education, research, and industrial fabric of the early 2010s. What we do not see is the substrate that will produce the next twenty years. That substrate appears in no ranking, because rankings are lagging indicators. By the time the score drops, the damage is already a decade old.

---

## What the rankings do not capture

Innovation has a physical and institutional underlay. Six building blocks will be decisive over the next ten years:

1. **Sovereign compute capacity.** Anyone serious about developing AI needs datacentres on home soil, with own energy and own hardware procurement. Switzerland has neither a strategic inventory nor a political target here.
2. **Supply-chain proximity.** Semiconductors, precision machines, specialty chemistry, critical raw materials. Distance from the source is a risk that shows up in no innovation indicator.
3. **Energy and manufacturing headroom.** Innovation does not scale without surplus energy capacity and manufacturing reserves. Both have become scarce across Europe.
4. **Talent inflow.** Top international researchers, engineers, and founders decide in life-years, not in legislative terms. Obstacles we erect today land in 2035.
5. **Anti-lock-in procurement.** When public administration, hospitals, and schools tie themselves to single vendors, innovation becomes a licence fee. Open standards and interchangeable components are a leading indicator of innovative capacity, not a footnote.
6. **Dense expertise clusters.** Research strength comes from neighbourhood, not subsidy. Clusters take decades to grow and dissolve faster than they form.

None of these six is visible in the GII score of 66.0.

---

## Where Switzerland is weak

The GII 2025 decomposes the overall score into seven pillars. Switzerland ranks first on Creative outputs, second on Knowledge and technology outputs, third on Institutions, third on Market sophistication, fifth on Infrastructure, fifth on Business sophistication. On Human capital and research, Switzerland ranks sixth.

That is the pillar that signals the next ten years. Education, doctorates, researchers per capita, public and private research spending. Precisely where the future is built, we are weakest.

A comparison of research intensity reveals the pattern. Switzerland spent 3.31 per cent of GDP on R&D in 2021, historically between 3.1 and 3.4 per cent. Sweden reached 3.57 per cent in 2024. Belgium 3.36 per cent. Austria 3.26 per cent. Sweden has overtaken us on research intensity. Belgium and Austria are within reach.

The European Innovation Scoreboard 2025 likewise places Switzerland first in Europe for the eighth consecutive year, with 169.3 points. But the score is slightly below the previous year. At regional level, Stockholm, Hovedstaden, and London now lead. Zurich is fourth, Ticino in the top ten.

---

## Patents say less than they appear to

Patents per million inhabitants, 2023 data: Korea 3,696, Japan 1,839, Switzerland 1,212, China 1,079, United States 824. We are clearly ahead of the United States. But Korea has three times as many patents per capita, and the United States produces around 518,000 patents in absolute terms against 11,000 for Switzerland. Scale matters, because research ecosystems live on critical mass.

Patents per capita are a vanity metric. They measure activity, not effect, and they capture neither open-source contributions nor industrial manufacturing capability nor standards-setting power. Israel, for example, appears in the statistics with around 170 patents per million, because its inventors mostly file abroad. Domestic innovative capacity is much higher.

---

## The window is closing

By the time lagging indicators degrade, it is too late to act. Switzerland has the lead today to build the substrate for the next twenty years. In ten to fifteen years, that window is shut.

Concretely: decisions on sovereign compute infrastructure, on talent policy, on procurement rules, on energy and manufacturing reserves, must be taken in this legislative term and the next. Later corrections are more expensive and slower, because clusters, supply chains, and talent flows have inertia. A university that loses its international pull does not regain it within one legislative term. A datacentre that does not exist cannot be built by decree.

---

## What this means for our programme

The Future has argued from the start for digital sovereignty grounded in open standards, transparency, and security. The substrate gap is the reason for that position, not a political slogan. Specifically, we call for:

- **Anti-lock-in as a procurement principle.** Federal, cantonal, and municipal procurement leaves vendor change always possible. Open data formats, documented interfaces, interchangeable components.
- **Sovereign compute capacity as a national objective.** An inventory of Swiss datacentre capacity, its energy connection, and its procurement paths, with measurable expansion targets.
- **Simpler talent inflow.** Researchers, engineers, and founders from third countries need shorter paths, not longer ones.
- **Maintain and increase research intensity.** 3.5 per cent of GDP as the next target, with a clear public component.
- **Create energy headroom.** Innovation and resilience need reserves, not scarcity.

These are not new demands. They are the consequence of a simple observation: the ranking we are proud of describes our past. The substrate we will be measured on is being built today.

---

## Further reading

This note is the civic translation of two companion articles published today, 1 May 2026:

- *Patents Per Capita Is a Vanity Metric* on [raskell.io](https://raskell.io/articles/patents-per-capita-is-a-vanity-metric/) (engineering perspective)
- *Europe Without Datacenters* on [archipelag.io](https://archipelag.io/news/europe-without-datacenters/) (industry and policy perspective)

Sources: [WIPO GII 2025](https://www.wipo.int/web-publications/global-innovation-index-2025/en/gii-2025-results.html), [Switzerland profile GII 2025](https://www.wipo.int/edocs/gii-ranking/2025/ch.pdf), [WIPI 2024](https://www.wipo.int/web-publications/world-intellectual-property-indicators-2024-highlights/en/patents-highlights.html), [World Bank R&D as % of GDP](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/GB.XPD.RSDV.GD.ZS?locations=CH), [European Innovation Scoreboard 2025](https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/knowledge-publications-tools-and-data/publications/all-publications/european-innovation-scoreboard-2025_en).

# Methodology

> Our editorial guardrails: evidence levels, correction policy, source transparency.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/methodik/ · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

## Editorial principles

The Future Lab publishes evidence-based analysis. Every note cites its sources, indicates the strength of evidence, and clearly distinguishes between data, interpretation, and policy positioning.

## Evidence levels

Every note receives one of three evidence levels:

- **Strong evidence**: Peer-reviewed studies, official statistics (FSO, SECO, OECD), replicated results.
- **Medium evidence**: Individual studies, working papers, official reports without peer review, consistent journalistic research.
- **Weak evidence**: Pilot data, models with uncertain assumptions, single-case observations. Marked as questions and prompts for discussion.

## Correction policy

Mistakes are inevitable — what matters is how they are handled. Factual errors are corrected immediately and the correction is documented at the end of the note. If the data changes significantly, the note is updated with a change notice.

## Update policy

Notes are never deleted. When data becomes outdated, a notice is added. Major reassessments result in a new note that references the original.

---

# Future Monitor

> Where does Switzerland stand on AI, robotics, open government and talent? The indicators behind our vision, with sources, targets and next update.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/monitor/ · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

As of 2026-11-08. Data: https://die-zukunft.ch/zukunftslabor/monitor.json (CC BY 4.0).

- **Industrial robot density** (robots per 10,000 employees): 2016: 128, 2020: 181 (unconfirmed), 2022: 296 (unconfirmed), 2024: 294. Target: about 600 by 2035. In 2024 the IFR switched to new Chinese employment data, so comparisons with earlier years are limited. Source: IFR World Robotics.
- **E-Government rank (UN)** (rank of 193 countries): 2003: 8, 2008: 12, 2010: 18, 2012: 15, 2014: 30, 2016: 28, 2018: 15, 2020: 16, 2022: 23, 2024: 26. Target: top 10 by 2030. The rank is relative: Switzerland's score rose in 2024, others improved faster. Source: UN DESA, E-Government Survey.
- **Publicly accessible AI compute** (GPUs in the Alps supercomputer (CSCS)): 2024: 10752. Target: ten times more by 2030. Alps is a research system of the ETH Domain, not freely accessible to business or government. A target in GPUs is an approximation. Source: CSCS.
- **Alps in the TOP500 list** (world rank): 2024: 6, 2024.5: 7, 2025: 8, 2025.5: 8, 2026: 10. Performance unchanged since November 2024 (434.9 PFlop/s); the drop comes from new systems elsewhere. Source: TOP500.
- **Data-centre electricity use** (% of Swiss electricity use): 2013: 2.8 (unconfirmed), 2019: 3.1, 2024: 3.6. 2024: 2.1 TWh. The SFOE expects 4.3 to 6 percent by 2030. Efficiency potential about 0.8 TWh. Source: BFE / EnergieSchweiz, Grundlagenbericht 2026.
- **Use of third-country permit quotas** (% of the 8,500 permits): 2020: 64, 2021: 77, 2022: 86 (unconfirmed), 2023: 78, 2024: 74. The quotas are not used up: the bottleneck is not the number of permits but attractiveness to top talent. Hence our talent visa. Source: SEM / Bundesrat.
- **Use of generative AI in the population** (% of the population (15–88)): 2025: 43. Source: BFS, Internetnutzung in den Haushalten 2025.
- **People working in agriculture** (people): 2000: 203793, 2005: 181092, 2010: 167462, 2015: 155304, 2020: 149521, 2024: 147876, 2025: 145628. Source: BFS, Landwirtschaftliche Strukturerhebung.
- **Manufacturing share of the economy** (% of GDP): 2015: 17.9, 2017: 18.4, 2019: 19.2, 2021: 20.7, 2023: 19.4, 2024: 19.1. Source: Weltbank (nationale Gesamtrechnung).

## Milestones

- [offen] National AI infrastructure strategy: recommended by the Science Council, Federal Council decision pending. (2026-05-12, https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/TuWsKZqat-kRc99SWg_nB)
- [in Arbeit] Motion for sovereign AI infrastructure passed by both chambers; the Federal Council must draft legislation. (2026-03-23, https://www.netzwoche.ch/news/2026-03-23/staenderat-sagt-ja-zu-souveraener-ki-infrastruktur)
- [in Arbeit] Open Swiss model: Apertus 1.0 (2025) and 1.5 (2026) released; use in the federal administration not yet decided. (2026-07-24, https://www.cscs.ch/science/computer-science-hpc/2026/apertus-15-building-the-next-generation-of-open-ai-infrastructure)
- [offen] Talent visa: does not exist. The Foreign Nationals Act revision (Parliament 2027) only eases job search after postdoc and higher vocational education. (2026-05-27, https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/CoWK1pRQ0MgU)
- [offen] Basic-income pilot: none running. Rejected at the ballot box in Zurich (2022) and Lucerne (2023); Bern has dropped it for now. (2026-10-19, https://www.plattformj.ch/artikel/247726/)
- [in Arbeit] e-ID: approved at the ballot box in 2025, launch postponed; trust infrastructure planned for the first half of 2027. (2026-06-30, https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/S-HhoNJa-wbO)
- [in Arbeit] AI regulation: consultation draft on the Council of Europe convention announced for end of 2026, not yet opened. (2025-02-12, https://www.bj.admin.ch/de/kuenstliche-intelligenz)

## Method

We use official sources (FSO, SFOE, SEM, UN, IFR, TOP500, CSCS) and flag values that come only from media reports or charts. Ranks are relative: a worse rank can also mean others improved faster. The data is available under CC BY 4.0 as [monitor.json](https://die-zukunft.ch/zukunftslabor/monitor.json). Found an error? [Tell us](@/kontakt.en.md); we correct publicly, as described in the [method](@/zukunftslabor/methodik.en.md).

# Artificial General Intelligence and the Labour Market: Two Scenarios for Switzerland

> How exposed Swiss occupations are to generative AI, how quickly the effects could arrive, and what transition policy a slow or a fast trajectory would require. Scenarios, not forecasts.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/agi-szenarien-arbeitsmarkt/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

According to the ILO, around a third of workers in high-income countries are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI; the IMF puts the figure for advanced economies at around 60%, of which roughly half is more likely to be complemented than replaced. In 2025 Switzerland had around 4.89 million employed persons; the most exposed group, clerical support workers, has already been shrinking for years. Nobody knows how fast this will accelerate: AI researchers put a 50% probability on machines performing every task better than humans by 2047. We therefore describe two scenarios and what each requires of policy.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

Employment by major occupational group (CH-ISCO-19) comes from the Swiss Labour Force Survey (SLFS) of the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), annual averages for 2010 and 2025. For exposure we rely on two studies: the ILO's refined index (Working Paper 140, 2025), which scores around 30,000 tasks, and the IMF Staff Discussion Note (2024), which additionally distinguishes whether AI is more likely to complement or to replace an activity. Neither study provides Swiss figures. Applying their averages to Switzerland is a **rough estimate**; Switzerland has an above-average share of professional and technical occupations. Exposure does not mean job loss: it measures which share of tasks could be automated or supported with today's technology. The two scenarios are planning assumptions, not forecasts.

---

### Where Switzerland works

The largest group is professionals, with around 1.3 million employed persons, followed by technicians and associate professionals (844,000). Clerical support workers number 571,000. According to the ILO, clerical occupations have the highest exposure: 8 of the 13 occupations in the highest tier (gradient 4) are clerical tasks such as accounting, payroll and data entry, alongside financial analysis, credit processing, call-centre sales, and web and multimedia development, among others. Roughly transferred, the high-income-country average (34% exposed, 17.3% in the two highest tiers) would mean around 1.7 million exposed jobs in Switzerland, of which around 850,000 are highly exposed (estimate).

---

### The shift is already under way

Between 2010 and 2025 the number of employed persons grew by 678,000. Over the same period clerical support workers lost 54,000 jobs and craft and related trades 118,000, while professionals gained 340,000 and technicians and associate professionals 245,000. So far the Swiss labour market has absorbed such shifts over 15 years. The decisive question is whether the next restructuring will allow as much time.

---

### How fast? The experts disagree

In the largest survey of 2,778 AI researchers (autumn 2023), the aggregate probability that machines will perform every task better than humans without human help is 10% by 2027 and 50% by 2047, 13 years earlier than in the 2022 survey. The same researchers expect full automation of all occupations much later: 50% only by 2116. The range is enormous. At the same time, the ILO urges caution: after two years of practice it lowered its automation scores for clerical tasks, because many activities require more human work than initially assumed.

---

### Two scenarios

**Scenario A: gradual diffusion.** AI capabilities keep improving, but adoption in firms takes years. The restructuring proceeds much as in 2010–2025: exposed groups shrink slowly, as clerical support workers have since 2010 at a little over half a percent per year, and new activities emerge alongside. Following the IMF's logic, just under half of exposed jobs (27% of all jobs in advanced economies) are more likely to be complemented than replaced by AI.

**Scenario B: rapid breakthrough.** Systems reach broad cognitive capability within about ten years, i.e. the early edge of the expert survey. The restructuring then hits the group with high exposure and low complementarity (33% of jobs in advanced economies according to the IMF, roughly 1.6 million in Switzerland when transferred, estimate) within a few years rather than decades. The problem is then less the number than the pace.

---

## What this means for policy

- **For scenario A:** continuously adapt in-company training and apprenticeship occupations, with a focus on clerical and administrative occupations; publish exposure and employment by occupation annually: [Work Without Fear](@/uebergaenge.en.md).
- **For scenario B:** prepared instruments that can be scaled up quickly: wage insurance for career changes, a tested basic income model as a foundation and a dividend from productivity gains: [Basic Income](@/grundeinkommen.en.md).
- **For both:** we plan for the early case without prophesying it. Leading indicators such as the quarterly SLFS data by occupation should determine when the scenario B instruments are triggered.

---

## Sources

1. Federal Statistical Office (FSO), SLFS: Berufshauptgruppen CH-ISCO-19 der Erwerbstätigen nach Nationalität [major occupational groups of employed persons by nationality] (T 03.02.01.21), 2010–2025. https://www.bfs.admin.ch/asset/de/36710074
2. Gmyrek, P. et al. (2025): Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure. ILO Working Paper 140. https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2025-05/WP140_web.pdf
3. Cazzaniga, M. et al. (2024): Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work. IMF Staff Discussion Note SDN/2024/001. https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/staff-discussion-notes/Issues/2024/01/14/Gen-AI-Artificial-Intelligence-and-the-Future-of-Work-542379
4. Grace, K. et al. (2025): Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 84. https://jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/19087

---

# AHV and VAT: what the numbers say about the 29 November proposal

> From 2026 the 13th AHV pension costs around CHF 4.1 billion a year. Together with the federal contribution, the 0.4-point VAT increase covers about half of it. The official figures on deficits, household burden and ageing, without a voting recommendation.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/ahv-mehrwertsteuer-zahlen/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

With the 13th pension, the AHV's pay-as-you-go result (Umlageergebnis) turns negative in 2026. According to the July 2026 financial projections of the Federal Social Insurance Office (FSIO/BSV), the shortfall is around CHF 1.3 billion in 2026 and, without additional financing, around CHF 4.9 billion in 2035. With the VAT increase that goes to the vote on 29 November, it would be around CHF 3.3 billion in 2035. According to the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV), an average household would pay around CHF 180 more per year. Underneath lies a demographic trend that none of the three FSO scenarios reverses: in 2025 there are 33 people aged 65 and over for every 100 people of working age; in 2050 there will be 43. We do not give a voting recommendation here.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

All AHV figures come from the FSIO financial projections of 2 July 2026, in millions of francs at constant 2025 prices. We show the **pay-as-you-go result**: current revenue minus expenditure, excluding returns on the AHV fund's investments. The FSIO calculates two variants: current law (13th pension from 2026, no additional financing) and the financing of the 13th pension as put to the vote (VAT +0.4 percentage points from 2028, reduced rate unchanged). The FSIO no longer publishes a variant **without the 13th pension**; we derive it by adding the cost of the 13th pension reported by the FSIO back to the current-law result and subtracting the federal contribution on it (20.2 per cent). This line is our own calculation and is marked as such. The household burden comes from the Federal Council's explanatory booklet (FTA estimate based on the 2018–2019 Household Budget Survey, HBS). Demography comes from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) scenarios 2025–2055.

---

### Deficits with and without the proposal

In 2025 the AHV closed with a pay-as-you-go surplus of CHF 1.84 billion. From 2026 the 13th pension costs CHF 4.1 billion a year according to the FSIO, and CHF 5.1 billion in 2035; the federal government bears 20.2 per cent of it. Under current law the result falls to –CHF 2.6 billion (2030) and –CHF 4.9 billion (2035). With the proposal, an additional CHF 1.1 billion flows into the AHV from 2028 and around CHF 1.4 to 1.5 billion a year from 2029; the deficit would then be –CHF 1.2 billion (2030) and –CHF 3.3 billion (2035). From 2029, VAT and the federal contribution together cover 50 to 52 per cent of the cost of the 13th pension (our calculation from the FSIO tables). The dashed line shows that without the 13th pension the result would lie roughly between –CHF 0.8 and +CHF 2.0 billion until 2040. The zigzag arises because pensions are adjusted every two years.

**The AHV fund.** The law requires the compensation fund to hold, as a rule, at least one year's expenditure (100 per cent). Under current law it falls to 99 per cent in 2027, 51 per cent in 2035 and 23 per cent in 2040, according to the FSIO. With the proposal it would be 68 per cent in 2035 and 53 per cent in 2040. The minimum reserve is therefore undershot in both variants.

**The range.** Besides the reference scenario, the FSIO calculates a favourable and an unfavourable scenario. Under current law, the 2035 result ranges from –CHF 8.3 billion (low) to –CHF 1.3 billion (high). The FSIO also expresses the 2035 reference deficit in VAT points: without the proposal it equals 1.2 points, with the proposal 0.8 points.

---

### What the increase costs a household

According to the FTA, the increase costs an average household around CHF 180 a year (CHF 15 a month). Households with a gross income of up to CHF 4,599 a month pay around CHF 7 more per month, households with CHF 6,700 to 9,399 around CHF 13, and households from CHF 13,400 around CHF 28. The booklet gives no values for the two intermediate classes; the light bars are a model: the FTA figures from the dispatch for +0.7 points, multiplied by 4/7. For the three official classes this simple conversion is 5 to 10 per cent above the official value, because the reduced rate does not rise this time. The model values are therefore probably too high.

In francs, high-income households pay more; measured against income, they pay less. For a 0.7-point increase, the FTA had calculated in the dispatch 0.41 per cent of gross income for the lowest fifth and 0.26 per cent for the highest. No percentage calculation has been published for the 0.4 points now adopted. At the same time, pensioners receive the 13th pension: up to CHF 2,520 a year for single people and up to CHF 3,780 for married couples.

---

### Demography: the trend beneath the numbers

In the FSO reference scenario, the old-age dependency ratio rises from 33.0 (2025) to 36.8 (2030), 40.9 (2040) and 43.3 (2050). Put differently: in 2025 there are around three people aged 20 to 64 for every person aged 65 and over; in 2050 around 2.3. The high and low scenarios are only 0.2 to 0.3 points away in 2050; they differ mainly in population size, hardly in age structure. Only the extreme variants open a wider range: between 38.6 and 52.8 in 2055. In the reference scenario the number of people aged 65 and over rises from 1.81 million (2025) to 2.67 million (2055), and the number aged 80 and over from 0.54 to 1.03 million.

The FSIO uses exactly this FSO scenario A-00-2025 for its reference scenario. Ageing is therefore already built into all the AHV figures above.

---

## What the numbers do not say

- **No certainty beyond 2035.** The FSIO itself states that projections beyond ten years are subject to great uncertainty. The range for 2035 runs from –CHF 1.3 to –CHF 8.3 billion.
- **No investment returns.** The pay-as-you-go result leaves out the AHV fund's returns; for the fund level, the FSIO assumes a real return of around 2 per cent. Good or bad market years shift the fund level noticeably.
- **Old consumption data.** The household figures are based on 2018–2019 prices and consumption. According to the booklet, the actual burden is likely to be somewhat higher. Pass-through to prices is also an assumption: firms do not always pass on an increase in full.
- **No net balance per household.** The figures show the burden of the tax, not the balance with the 13th pension. Whether a household gains on balance depends on whether, and how much, AHV pension it receives.
- **Open parameters.** Whether the special rate for accommodation continues beyond 2027 was still open when the booklet went to press. The Federal Council intends to present the AHV2030 reform in spring 2027; it will change the projections.
- **No verdict on the right financing.** The figures show how large the gap is and who bears how much. Whether VAT, wage contributions, federal funds or benefit adjustments are the right path is a political question, not a statistical one.

---

## Context

Our reading of the four proposals of 29 November, also without a voting recommendation, is in the article [29 November 2026 vote](@/aktuelles/abstimmung-29-november-2026.en.md). Why we care about financing social insurance through consumption rather than through wages alone is explained in the [Basic Income](@/grundeinkommen.en.md) pillar; how different tax bases affect income distribution is shown in the note [Basic Income: Three Financing Models Compared](@/zukunftslabor/notizen/grundeinkommen-finanzierungsmodelle.en.md).

---

## Sources

1. Federal Social Insurance Office (FSIO/BSV): Financial situation and outlook of the AHV, financial projections of 2 July 2026. https://www.bsv.admin.ch/finanzen-ahv
2. FSIO: AHV financial projections under current law (reference, low and high scenarios), 2 July 2026. https://www.bsv.admin.ch/dam/de/sd-web/op2mTMWV0HCj/Finanzperspektiven%20der%20AHV%20gem%C3%A4ss%20geltender%20Ordnung.xlsx
3. FSIO: AHV financial projections with financing of the 13th pension (incl. "Massnahmen" sheet), 2 July 2026. https://www.bsv.admin.ch/dam/de/sd-web/jnnnev0Cvqna/Finanzperspektiven%20der%20AHV%20gem%C3%A4ss%20Finanzierung%20der%2013.%20Altersrente.xlsx
4. FSIO: Key facts: financial projections of the AHV, IV and EO with scenarios, 2 July 2026. https://www.bsv.admin.ch/dam/de/sd-web/layXpeKUCS4Y/Faktenblatt%20Szenarien_2026_DE.pdf

9. FSO: Projections – reference scenario 2025–2055 (fact sheet). https://dam-api.bfs.admin.ch/hub/api/dam/assets/34687124/master
