# Automation: How AI Is Shifting the Risk Map

> LLM-capable AI changes automation risk: office jobs are more exposed, manual work less so.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/automatisierungsrisiko-branchen/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

LLM-capable AI shifts automation risk: office jobs (finance, law,
administration) are more exposed than before 2018, manual occupations
less so. Around 1.27 million jobs are at post-LLM risk.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

FSO SLFS employment data (2024) and two risk models:
pre-LLM based on the OECD study by Nedelkoska & Quintini (2018, routine
tasks, building on Frey & Osborne 2013) and post-LLM based on the IMF
(Cazzaniga et al. 2024, AI exposure). The industry values are our own
rounded model assumptions derived from these studies; the studies themselves
do not report values by Swiss economic sector. Exposed jobs = employed
persons × risk share.

---

### Employment by industry

The industry structure provides the context: health and social work, manufacturing and retail employ the most people. The distribution shows which sectors would feel the largest absolute effects of an automation surge.

---

### Pre- vs. post-LLM

LLM-capable AI fundamentally shifts the risk map: industries such as finance and insurance, public administration and information/communication are considerably more exposed post-LLM than in the classic routine model. Manual occupations (construction, transport, hospitality), by contrast, are less exposed post-LLM.

---

### Risk shift

The shift shows the direction and extent of the change. Positive values mean increased risk due to LLMs. Office jobs rise the most — a signal that classic retraining programmes for manual occupations alone are not enough and that knowledge work must also come into focus.

---

### Exposed jobs

Absolute numbers show the social scale: industries with many employees and high post-LLM risk each account for tens of thousands to almost 190,000 potentially exposed jobs. This does not necessarily mean job losses — but it does mean transitions need to be managed systematically.

---

## Limitations

- Risk values by industry are modelled (our own assumptions based on the OECD and IMF), not measured values
- Risk estimates are industry averages, not occupation-specific
- Post-LLM estimates are provisional (LLM capabilities are evolving quickly)
- Actual job losses depend on regulation and complementarity

---

## Data sources

- FSO SLFS 2024: Erwerbstätige nach Wirtschaftsabschnitt [employed persons by economic section]
- OECD: Automation Risk by Occupation (Nedelkoska/Quintini 2018)
- Frey & Osborne (2013): The Future of Employment (basis of the OECD approach)
- IMF: AI Preparedness Index 2024 (Cazzaniga et al.)

---

# The Digital Readiness Gap: The Population Is Online — the State Is Not

> 90% of Swiss residents use the internet, but e-government and open data lag behind the EU average. The problem is not technological — it is institutional.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/digitale-souveraenitaet-luecke/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

90% of the Swiss population use the internet regularly — but
e-government use, online availability and open-data maturity lag
behind the EU average. The readiness gap between the digital
population and the digital state was 13.2 percentage points in 2025.
In 2021 a private-sector e-ID model was rejected at the ballot box
(64.4% no); the state-run e-ID was accepted only narrowly on
28 September 2025 (50.4% yes).

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

The analysis combines two FSO Omnibus ICT datasets (2014–2025):
internet use by age group (e-mail as a proxy) and
e-government use by type of service. The "readiness gap" is the
difference between general internet use and e-government use across
the whole population. Supplemented by the EU Open Data Maturity Report 2025, the VOX
post-vote survey (gfs.bern) on the 2021 e-ID referendum and the official
results of the 2021 and 2025 e-ID votes.

---

### Internet use by age group

The 15–29 and 30–59 age groups are at around 95% internet use. Even among those over 60, almost 80% are now online. The problem is not the population's digital skills — it is the missing digital infrastructure on the state's side.

---

### E-government use

E-government use rose from 67% (2014) to 82% (2023) but fell back to 77% in 2025 — even though internet use kept rising. This points to a supply problem: what is missing is not demand but usable digital services.

---

### Readiness gap

The gap between general internet use and e-government use stood at around 13 percentage points in 2025, after narrowing to 8 points by 2021. This readiness gap is not a technological but an institutional problem: the population is ready — the state is not.

---

### E-ID referendum: a question of trust

The 2021 no to the e-ID (64.4%) was aimed above all at the private-sector model: in the VOX post-vote survey, no voters most often cited data protection and data security (60% of all mentions) and the role of the state (49%), for example "the e-ID should be issued by the state" (25%). The redesigned, state-run e-ID was accepted with 50.4% yes on 28 September 2025. The narrow result shows that trust in data protection and state responsibility is a precondition for digital identity, not a given.

---

### Open-data maturity

In the Open Data Maturity Report 2025, Switzerland scores 82% (2 points more than in 2024) and belongs to the "followers" cluster (73–84%). The EU-27 average is 86%, and France leads with 100%. There is progress, such as the "open by default" principle in the EMBAG act and the OGD master plan 2024–2027, but the distance to the leading countries remains. This hampers innovation, transparency and evidence-based policymaking.

---

## Limitations

- E-mail use as a proxy for internet use (FSO definition)
- E-government data not available by age group — gap can only be calculated at total level
- Open-data score based on EU methodology (Switzerland as a participating EFTA country)
- E-ID motives: VOX post-vote survey with a limited sample, open question with multiple answers

---

## Data sources

- FSO Omnibus ICT 2014–2025: internet use, e-government use
- data.europa.eu: Open Data Maturity Report 2025, https://data.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-12/2025_odm_report_7.pdf
- data.europa.eu: Open Data Maturity 2025, country factsheet Switzerland, https://data.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-12/2025_odm_factsheet_switzerland.pdf
- gfs.bern: VOX analysis March 2021 (e-ID act, in German), https://swissvotes.ch/vote/639.00/nachbefragung-de.pdf
- Swissvotes: e-ID act of 7 March 2021, rejected with 64.4% no, https://swissvotes.ch/vote/639.00
- SRF: vote of 28 September 2025, e-ID act accepted with 50.4% yes, https://www.srf.ch/news/schweiz/abstimmungen-28-september-so-hat-die-schweiz-abgestimmt

---

# From 16th to 26th: Why Switzerland Is Falling Behind in E-Government

> In the UN E-Government Development Index, Switzerland fell from 16th (2020) to 23rd (2022) and 26th (2024). Infrastructure and education are strong; the gap lies in the state's online services.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/egovernment-rang-26/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

In the United Nations E-Government Development Index (EGDI), Switzerland fell from 16th place (2020) via 23rd (2022) to 26th (2024) out of 193 countries, even though its index score rose slightly (0.89 to 0.90). Other countries are simply improving faster. In infrastructure and education Switzerland is close to the top; the gap lies almost entirely in the state's online services. The state e-ID, narrowly approved in September 2025, has had no launch date since June 2026.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

The EGDI is the average of three equally weighted sub-indices between 0 and 1: the Online Service Index (OSI, supply and quality of public online services), the Telecommunication Infrastructure Index (TII) and the Human Capital Index (HCI). All values come from the country profiles of the UN E-Government Knowledge Base (surveys 2018–2024). We compare Switzerland, Denmark, Estonia, South Korea, Singapore, Germany and Austria. Important: in 2024 the UN adjusted the methodology (TII with affordability instead of fixed broadband, HCI with an additional e-government literacy component). Absolute values are therefore only partly comparable across years; ranks within a given survey year are comparable.

---

### A decline at a high level

Switzerland ranked 15th in 2018, 16th in 2020, 23rd in 2022 and 26th in 2024. Its EGDI score remained almost stable (2020: 0.8907; 2022: 0.8752; 2024: 0.9004). The decline is therefore relative: Switzerland is stagnating, while countries such as Singapore (2022: 12th, 2024: 3rd), Estonia (8th to 2nd) and Germany (22nd to 12th) are making clear gains. Austria fell from 20th to 22nd over the same period.

---

### The gap lies with the state, not the population

In telecommunications infrastructure (0.958) and human capital (0.903), Switzerland is among the leading countries. On the Online Service Index, by contrast, it scores only 0.841, compared with 0.999 (Denmark), 0.995 (Estonia), 1.000 (South Korea) and 0.983 (Singapore). Germany (0.924) is also clearly ahead; only Austria (0.838) is similarly weak. Switzerland's OSI was 0.829 in 2020 and 0.768 in 2022. This shows that the networks and education are in place; what is missing is the administration's digital offering.

---

### Where exactly the Online Service Index loses points

On the institutional framework (strategies, laws), Switzerland, like all comparison countries, achieves the maximum score. The gaps arise in implementation: service provision 0.81 (Estonia 1.00, Denmark 0.99), content 0.89 (Estonia and Denmark 1.00), e-participation 0.82 and above all technology 0.63 (all three comparison countries 0.88). Switzerland, in other words, has the papers but too few end-to-end digital procedures.

---

### E-ID: approved, but without a launch date

Voters approved the e-ID Act on 28 September 2025 with 50.4% in favour. In February 2026 the Confederation named 1 December 2026 as the launch date. On 30 June 2026 it withdrew this date: because of new AI risks (deepfakes, malware on end devices), online issuance is to be additionally secured. There is no new date; the trust infrastructure is to go into operation in the first half of 2027. The reasons are understandable, but the consequence for the index is clear: without a widely used digital identity, end-to-end online procedures remain the exception.

### What the leading countries do differently

- **A shared data exchange layer:** in Estonia, X-Road connects public and private registers; according to e-Estonia, around 2.2 billion transactions run through it each year. Authorities query data from one another instead of asking the population for it again (once-only).
- **Digital identity in everyday life:** Singpass has 5 million users and over 41 million transactions per month; with Myinfo, forms are pre-filled automatically.
- **Digital channel as the default:** in Denmark, residents and businesses are legally required to be able to receive Digital Post; those who cannot communicate digitally continue to receive paper.

Switzerland has a foundation too: since 1 January 2024 the EMBAG (Federal Act on the Use of Electronic Means for the Performance of Official Tasks) has applied, with the principle of "open by default" for government data; the transition period for this ends at the end of 2026.

---

## What this means for policy

- **Make the goal measurable:** back into the top 15 by the 2028 UN survey, measured by the Online Service Index, not by strategy papers: [Open Government](@/offener-staat.en.md).
- **Enshrine once-only in law:** data that one authority already holds may not be requested again by another; exchange takes place via documented interfaces (API by default).
- **E-ID with a timetable:** document the security work openly and publish a binding launch date with milestones.
- **Meet the EMBAG deadline:** from 2027, publicly report which federal offices actually make their data openly available.

---

## Sources

1. UN DESA, E-Government Knowledge Base: country profile Switzerland (surveys 2020, 2022, 2024). https://publicadministration.un.org/egovkb/en-us/Data/Country-Information/id/166-Switzerland
2. UN DESA, country profiles Denmark, Estonia, South Korea, Singapore, Germany, Austria (2024 survey). https://publicadministration.un.org/egovkb/en-us/Data/Country-Information/id/48-Denmark (likewise id/57, 138, 154, 65, 10)
3. UN DESA: E-Government Survey 2024 (methodology, Technical Appendix). https://publicadministration.un.org/egovkb/en-us/Reports/UN-E-Government-Survey-2024
4. Federal Council: e-ID Act, popular vote of 28 September 2025. https://www.admin.ch/en/e-id-act
5. FDJP: Akzeptanz der E-ID mit zusätzlichen Massnahmen stärken [strengthening acceptance of the e-ID with additional measures], 25 February 2026. https://www.ejpd.admin.ch/de/newnsb/L6Nbf7gStnDm
6. Federal Office of Justice: Neuer Zeitplan für die Einführung der E-ID und der Vertrauensinfrastruktur [new timetable for the introduction of the e-ID and the trust infrastructure], 30 June 2026. https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/4ZNYpSk3J1-U
7. e-Estonia: X-Road. https://e-estonia.com/solutions/interoperability-services/x-road/
8. GovTech Singapore: Singpass. https://www.tech.gov.sg/products-and-services/for-citizens/digital-services/singpass/
9. Agency for Digital Government (Denmark): Digital Post. https://en.digst.dk/systems/digital-post/
10. FSO: Open Government Data, EMBAG Art. 10 and Masterplan 2024–2027. https://www.bfs.admin.ch/de/strategie-og-de

# Electricity Stress Test: What Happens with Drought plus a Nuclear Phase-Out?

> Four scenarios show how vulnerable Switzerland's electricity supply is — from the baseline to the worst case of drought combined with a nuclear shutdown.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/energieresilienz-stressszenarien/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Four stress scenarios based on real SFOE data (2024) show that
in the worst case (dry year + nuclear phase-out) Switzerland would
have to import 39.1% of its electricity — at a cost of
around CHF 2.07 billion per year at EUR 90/MWh.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

The basis is the SFOE electricity balance (OGD, 2024). Four scenarios
modify the production figures of the base year:

- **A — Baseline**: actual production in 2024
- **B — Dry year**: −30% hydropower production (historically plausible, e.g. 2022)
- **C — Nuclear phase-out**: nuclear power plants shut down (−22,983 GWh)
- **D — Combined**: dry year + nuclear phase-out

Import costs calculated at EUR 90/MWh (European average spot price 2023–2024) and
an exchange rate of CHF 0.95 per EUR, i.e. around CHF 86/MWh.
Final energy consumption by sector from the SFOE overall energy balance.

---

### Electricity mix

Hydropower and nuclear energy dominate Swiss electricity production, together accounting for over 90%. This concentration on two sources is both a strength (dispatchable domestic production) and a vulnerability — both are sensitive to external shocks: drought for hydropower, political decisions for nuclear.

---

### Final energy consumption by sector

Transport and households are the largest final energy consumers (all energy carriers, not just electricity). The sectoral distribution shows where efficiency gains and electrification (e.g. electric mobility) have the greatest leverage — and where additional electricity demand will arise.

---

### Stress scenarios

Four scenarios show the range of vulnerability: from the stable baseline to the worst case (dry year + nuclear phase-out). The combined scenario creates an import dependence that cannot easily be covered when European markets are tight. Scenario C is a stress test, not a forecast: the current Nuclear Energy Act prohibits new nuclear power plants, while the existing ones may run as long as they are safe. In August 2025 the Federal Council proposed lifting the ban on new plants as an indirect counter-proposal to the popular initiative "Blackout stoppen" (stop the blackout). How long today's plants will run and whether new ones will be built remains politically open.

---

### Import costs

The financial consequences of import dependence are considerable: in the worst case, annual import costs amount to around CHF 2.1 billion — calculated at EUR 90/MWh and CHF 0.95 per EUR. Any deviation in the exchange rate shifts the costs proportionally. At market peaks (as in 2022), the costs would be a multiple of that.

---

## Limitations

- Static scenarios (no expansion of solar/wind, no reduction in demand)
- Import prices fluctuate strongly (2022: up to EUR 400/MWh); EUR/CHF exchange rate as a fixed assumption (0.95)
- Data basis 2024; the SFOE electricity balance 2025 has not yet been incorporated
- Seasonal effects not modelled (winter gap > annual average)
- No storage effects (pumped storage, batteries)

---

## Data sources

- SFOE: Swiss electricity balance (OGD, annual figures)
- SFOE: Swiss overall energy balance (final energy consumption by sector)
- ENTSO-E: European electricity prices (day-ahead spot market)
- Federal Council: press release of 13 August 2025 on the dispatch on the "Blackout stoppen" initiative and the indirect counter-proposal (lifting the ban on new nuclear power plants, in German), https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/GIECKzWVs6ZX6W1ba4i6X

---

# Research: Who Does It, Who Pays — and What Comes Back?

> Switzerland invests heavily in R&D and files the most European patent applications per capita. But the private sector dominates — and the question of the public return on public research remains open.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/forschung-wer-forscht-wer-zahlt/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Switzerland invests CHF 25.6 billion in R&D
(2023) and, with 182 EPO patents per billion, achieves the
highest patent efficiency among the countries compared. But private-sector research outweighs public
research by a factor of 2.37 — and the top 2 sectors
account for 45.4% of spending.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

The basis is the FSO research statistics (intramural R&D expenditure by sector,
2000–2023) and EPO patent data (Annual Report 2023). The
private sector comprises pharma, metallurgy, ICT, instruments and other
industrial sectors. Public: universities, the ETH Domain, federal offices.

---

### R&D expenditure over time

The private sector dominates R&D expenditure, but its lead has narrowed since 2000 (private-to-public ratio: 3.1 → 2.4) and has only been growing slightly again since 2017. This demonstrates innovative strength — but also a dependence: when a few large corporations finance most of the research, blind spots emerge on topics without a direct market incentive.

---

### Private vs. public

In Switzerland the private sector spends considerably more on R&D than the public sector (2023: 2.4 to 1). On the one hand, this is a sign of a research-intensive private sector — on the other, it raises the question of whether public research carries enough weight of its own to cover basic research and public-interest topics.

---

### Patent efficiency in international comparison

Among the countries compared, Switzerland achieves the highest patent efficiency: more EPO patent applications per billion invested than Sweden, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria, France, the USA and Japan. According to the EPO (Technology Dashboard 2025), Switzerland also files the most European patent applications per capita among countries with more than one million inhabitants. This points to an effective chain from research to usable knowledge — a locational advantage that needs to be maintained.

---

### Sector concentration

One sector — chemicals/pharma — accounts for around a third of private R&D, and together with ICT for almost half. This makes the research landscape vulnerable: the relocation of a single company could shift the overall statistics markedly. Diversifying the research base is a strategic question.

---

## Limitations

- FSO data collected every 2 years (no annual values)
- Patent efficiency: EPO patents as a proxy (not all innovations result in patents); selection of eight countries
- Patent data as of 2023; the EPO figures for 2025 (Technology Dashboard 2025, successor to the Patent Index) have not yet been incorporated
- Private R&D expenditure partly estimated (trade secrets)
- Sector classification follows FSO logic (Frascati Manual)

---

## Data sources

- FSO: Forschung und Entwicklung — Intramuros-Aufwendungen [research and development — intramural expenditure] (2000–2023)
- EPO: Annual Report 2023 — patent applications by country of origin
- OECD: Main Science and Technology Indicators (GERD)
- EPO: Technology Dashboard 2025 (patent applications per capita), https://www.epo.org/en/about-us/statistics/technology-dashboard-2025

---

# Health Costs: Where Does the Money Go — and Where Does It Drain Away?

> In 2024 the Swiss health system cost CHF 97.2 billion, 4.4% of which went to administration (FSO). By the OECD definition the share is 5.2%, above the OECD average of 3.3%.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/gesundheitskosten-verwaltung-fokus/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

The Swiss health system cost CHF 97.2 billion in 2024
(2023: CHF 93.4 billion), of which CHF 4.24 billion or 4.4% went to
administration (FSO). By the OECD definition, Switzerland's 5.2% is above
the OECD average (3.3%). The difference corresponds to around CHF 17 per
person per month.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

FSO statistics on the costs and financing of the health system according to
the System of Health Accounts (SHA). The long series 1995–2019 is based on
the methodology before the FSO revision of April 2025; revised figures are
available for 2019, 2023 and 2024 and are shown separately (2024 provisional).
Categories: outpatient/inpatient curative care, long-term care, medical goods,
administration, prevention. International comparison based on OECD Health at
a Glance 2023 (OECD definition, not identical to the FSO figures).

---

### Expenditure by category over time

Health expenditure is rising continuously — but not evenly. Outpatient and inpatient care account for the lion's share. Administrative costs almost doubled between 1995 and 2019 (CHF 1.7 → 3.3 billion, old FSO methodology), but grew more slowly than total spending. Under the revised methodology they stood at CHF 4.24 billion in 2024; in 2023 they rose by 9.6%, much faster than total costs. The open question is how much of the rise in premiums goes into treatment and how much into bureaucracy.

---

### Administrative share over time

By the old FSO definition, the administrative share fell from around 5% (1995) to 4% (2019). Under the revised methodology it is somewhat higher: 4.1% (2019), 4.5% (2023) and 4.4% (2024). In the OECD comparison it remains high: the insurance landscape with 42 health insurers (2025, FOPH) generates structural extra costs — accounting, marketing, risk selection — part of which would not arise in a simpler system.

---

### International comparison

By the OECD definition (5.2%), Switzerland's administrative costs are well above the OECD average (3.3%); by the FSO definition the share is 4.4%. Countries with more centralised systems (e.g. Sweden) achieve lower administrative shares with comparable or better quality of care. The comparison shows that efficiency gains are possible.

---

### Administrative excess

The 1.9 percentage-point gap to the OECD average corresponds to around CHF 17 per person per month when applied to the FSO's 2024 health costs of CHF 899 per capita per month. Using the FSO administrative share (4.4%), it is around CHF 10. This money does not go into treatment, medicines or care — it finances administrative structures whose simplification would lower premiums.

---

## Limitations

- SHA harmonisation facilitates comparisons, but differences between systems remain
- FSO revision 2025: figures before and after the revision are not directly comparable; 2024 figures provisional
- OECD and FSO definitions of administrative costs differ (5.2% vs. 4.4%); the franc amounts combine OECD shares with FSO total costs
- Administrative costs also include quality assurance and regulatory effort
- Single-payer vs. competitive model produce structurally different administrative costs
- OECD data partly from different years (2021–2023)

---

## Data sources

- FSO: Kosten und Finanzierung des Gesundheitswesens 2023 [costs and financing of the health system 2023], press release of 28 April 2025, https://dam-api.bfs.admin.ch/hub/api/dam/assets/34788155/master
- FSO: Kosten des Gesundheitswesens nach Leistung [health costs by service] (2019, 2023, 2024), https://www.bfs.admin.ch/asset/de/36519541
- FSO: Kosten des Gesundheitswesens seit 1960 [health costs since 1960], https://www.bfs.admin.ch/asset/de/36519640
- FSO: health costs and financing 2024 (CHF 97.2 billion, CHF 899 per capita per month), https://www.bfs.admin.ch/asset/de/36515499
- FSO: Kosten und Finanzierung des Gesundheitswesens [costs and financing of the health system] (series 1995–2019, methodology before 2025)
- FOPH: Tätigkeitsbericht 2025 soziale Kranken- und Unfallversicherung [2025 activity report, number of insurers], https://www.bag.admin.ch/dam/en/sd-web/TiFIhRVtPuIx/BAG_Ta%CC%88tigkeitsbericht_2025_soziale-Kranken-und-Unfallversicherung.pdf
- OECD: Health at a Glance 2023 — Health Expenditure and Financing
- WHO: Global Health Expenditure Database

---

# Basic Income: Three Financing Models Compared

> What happens to the income distribution if a UBI is financed through income tax, replacement of transfers or a consumption tax? A decile simulation with FSO data.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/grundeinkommen-finanzierungsmodelle/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Three financing models for an unconditional basic income of CHF 2,500/month
show fundamentally different distributional effects. A flat income tax
reduces the Gini coefficient the most. Replacing existing transfers saves taxes,
but does the least for the poorest households — a non-trivial finding.
A consumption tax has a progressive effect, but a weaker one.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

The basis is the decile shares of disposable equivalised income from
the FSO table "Kennzahlen zur Verteilung der Einkommen" [key figures on
income distribution] (data basis 2018, Household Budget Survey HBS). From
these, absolute disposable equivalised incomes per decile and month are
estimated (share × mean × 10).

Three financing scenarios are simulated:

- **A — Flat income tax**: gross costs (CHF 222 billion/year)
  are financed through a linear income tax surcharge.
- **B — Replacement of transfers**: AHV/AVS (old-age and survivors' insurance), IV/AI (disability insurance), EL/PC (supplementary benefits), social assistance, ALV/AC (unemployment insurance) and family allowances
  (CHF 79 billion) are replaced by the UBI.
  The remaining amount is financed through income tax.
- **C — Consumption tax**: financing is through a VAT surcharge.
  Consumption ratios vary by decile (D1: 95%, D10: 55%).

The model is static: it ignores behavioural responses such as changes in
labour supply, consumption patterns or tax avoidance. The results show
first-round effects only.

---

### Baseline: income distribution 2018

Today's income distribution shows strong concentration: the top decile has just over a fifth (22%) of total disposable equivalised income, the bottom decile less than 3%. This baseline is the starting point for all three scenarios — it shows the initial situation from which redistribution takes effect.

---

### Net effect of the three scenarios

The three financing models have fundamentally different effects. Scenario A (income tax) redistributes linearly — lower deciles gain, upper deciles lose. Scenario B (replacement of transfers) produces a paradox: the lowest deciles gain the least in net terms (D1: +CHF 92/month) because the basic income largely just replaces their existing transfers. Scenario C (consumption tax) weighs relatively more heavily on lower deciles through their higher consumption ratio; thanks to the basic income, they still gain clearly in net terms.

---

### Gini coefficient by scenario

The Gini coefficient measures income concentration (0 = perfect equality, 1 = total inequality). Scenario A reduces the Gini the most, because progressive financing redistributes directly. Scenario B barely changes it, because it merely replaces existing transfers. Scenario C also lowers it markedly (from 0.28 to 0.18), but less than A: the consumption tax itself weighs relatively more on low incomes, and the basic income more than offsets this.

---

### Relative winners and losers

This shows which deciles gain or lose in net terms. The turning point varies depending on the financing model. The transfer paradox is most evident in scenario B: deciles 1–2, which depend heavily on existing social benefits, benefit less than the middle class — a counter-intuitive result that is decisive for political implementation.

---

## Limitations

- Aggregated decile data instead of microdata (individual data require an application to the FSO)
- No behavioural responses modelled (labour supply, consumption patterns, tax avoidance): static first-round effects
- Distribution of transfers across deciles estimated (not taken directly from SILC microdata)
- Consumption ratios by decile based on values from the literature, not HBS detail
- Data basis 2018: the FSO table series used ends in 2018; more recent HBS and SILC waves have not yet been incorporated

---

## Data sources

- FSO: Kennzahlen zur Verteilung der Einkommen vor und nach staatlichen Transfers [key figures on income distribution before and after state transfers] (HBS, data basis 2018), decile shares of disposable equivalised income, https://www.bfs.admin.ch/bfsstatic/dam/assets/15344786/master
- FSIO social insurance statistics: transfer volumes AHV, IV, EL, ALV
- FSO SILC: published distribution shares of social transfers

---

# Rent Burden: How Hard Do Rents Hit the Bottom Quintile in Each Canton?

> The bottom quintile spends 40% on rent — and, measured against cantonal rents, is already above the 30% threshold in every canton.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/mietbelastung-kantonale-prognose/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

The bottom quintile spends 40% on rent. Measured against cantonal rents,
it was already above the 30% threshold in all 26 cantons in 2023 — from 33% in Jura to 65% in Zug.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

FSO rent statistics (2010–2023, 3-room flats by canton) and
FSO SILC rent burden ratios. CAGR from the 2010/2023 ratio.

---

### Rent burden by income quintile

The bottom quintile spends around 40% of disposable income on rent — far above the 30% threshold that is considered critical. The upper quintiles are at 12–18%. The rent burden acts like a regressive tax: those who earn less pay proportionally more.

---

### Rents by canton

The differences between cantons are considerable: Zug, Zurich and Schwyz are at the top, rural cantons well below. The chart shows the price range of an average 3-room flat — the most common type of dwelling in Switzerland.

---

### Rent growth (CAGR)

Annual rent growth (CAGR) varies widely between cantons. Some cantons are growing twice as fast as others — and with real wages stagnating at the same time, a widening gap emerges. The pace of growth determines how quickly the burden keeps rising if incomes do not keep up.

---

## Limitations

- CAGR describes the 2010–2023 trend, not a forecast
- Q1 income not differentiated by canton
- Existing rents (rents for new tenancies are often higher)

---

## Data sources

- FSO Structural Survey: rents by canton and number of rooms
- FSO SILC 2022: rent burden ratio by quintile

---

# Compute and Electricity: What Ten Times More Public AI Capacity Would Require

> In 2024 data centres used around 2.1 TWh, or 3.6% of Swiss electricity. By our estimate, a tenfold increase in public compute based on Alps would require 0.6 to 0.8 TWh per year: manageable with planning, but not as an afterthought.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/rechenkraft-und-strom/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Switzerland's data centres consumed around 2.1 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, 3.6% of national consumption. By 2030 the Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE) expects 2.5 to 3.2 TWh, and 3.5 TWh in its maximum scenario. The country's largest public AI computer, Alps at CSCS in Lugano, drew around 7.1 megawatts during its official performance measurement. By our estimate, ten times as much public compute with today's technology would require 0.6 to 0.8 TWh per year, i.e. just over 1% of today's final consumption.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

We combine three official or primary sources: the SwissEnergy/SFOE study on the electricity consumption of data centres (May 2026), the SFOE's 2025 electricity balance and the measured power draw of Alps in the TOP500 list (7,124 kW, Level 3 measurement). Alps comprises 10,752 NVIDIA GH200 superchips in 2,688 nodes (CSCS).

The projection for a tenfold increase is **our own estimate** with deliberately simple assumptions: continuous operation for 8,760 hours per year at the measured Linpack power, scaled linearly. For cooling and building services we assume a 30% surcharge (PUE 1.3); this is an assumption, not a measured value for Alps. Newer chips deliver more computing power per watt, so the estimate is more of an upper bound for "ten times Alps".

---

### Data centres are growing, but predictably

Between 2019 and 2024, data centre consumption rose from 1.77 to 2.1 TWh, by an average of 3.4% per year. The growth comes from the large commercial data centres (44% of consumption), whose demand could more than double by 2030. In-house corporate data centres (56%) are stagnating or declining as workloads move to the cloud. The SFOE puts the remaining efficiency potential at around 0.8 TWh, almost 38% of today's consumption.

---

### The starting point on the grid

In 2025 Switzerland generated 67.5 TWh of electricity, with final consumption of 58.0 TWh (up 0.8% on 2024). 55.5% came from hydropower, of which 31.3 percentage points from storage power plants, 27.2% from nuclear energy and 11.8% from photovoltaics. The annual balance, however, says little about winter: data centres run all year round at an almost constant load, including when domestic production is scarce.

---

### What a tenfold increase would cost, in electricity

Calculation (estimate): 7.124 MW × 8,760 h gives around 62 GWh per year for Alps. Ten times that is 71 MW and 0.62 TWh; with a 30% cooling surcharge, 93 MW and 0.81 TWh. This corresponds to 1.1 to 1.4% of final consumption in 2025, less than the increase the SFOE already expects for all data centres by 2030 in its high scenario (+1.1 TWh), and roughly as much as the efficiency potential of existing data centres identified by the SFOE. For comparison: according to the International Energy Agency, a typical AI data centre consumes as much electricity as 100,000 households, and the largest ones under construction twenty times as much.

---

## What this means for policy

- **Plan energy and compute together.** A public AI programme of the order of 70 to 90 MW is feasible for the Swiss grid, but it needs fixed sites with grid connection, cooling and waste-heat recovery. This belongs in the same planning as the expansion of winter production: [Energy & Infrastructure Resilience](@/energy-resilience.en.md).
- **Realise efficiency first.** The identified efficiency potential of around 0.8 TWh in existing data centres corresponds roughly to the estimated demand of a tenfold increase in public compute. Binding efficiency metrics for large data centres free up room on the grid.
- **Expand public compute measurably.** Report targets and progress in megawatts and computing power, with open access for universities, SMEs and the administration: [Sovereign AI & Compute](@/souveraene-ki.en.md).

---

## Sources

1. Swiss Federal Office of Energy / SwissEnergy: Stromverbrauch der Rechenzentren in der Schweiz [electricity consumption of data centres in Switzerland], press release of 7 May 2026. https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/GV-_d7OgIlqjfQDGZqbkN
2. Swiss Federal Office of Energy: Elektrizitätsbilanz 2025 [electricity balance 2025], press release of 18 June 2026. https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/YQtEZcK-D9fQ
3. TOP500: Alps, HPE Cray EX254n, CSCS (power draw 7,124 kW, lists November 2024 to June 2026). https://www.top500.org/system/180259/
4. CSCS: Alps hardware (2,688 nodes, 10,752 GH200). https://docs.cscs.ch/alps/hardware/
5. International Energy Agency (IEA): Energy and AI, Executive Summary, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/executive-summary

---

# Doubling Robot Density: What 600 Instead of 294 Robots Would Mean

> Switzerland has 294 industrial robots per 10,000 employees, fewer than Germany or Japan. Research shows that more robots raise productivity. Whether jobs are lost depends heavily on how the transition is organised.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/roboterdichte-verdoppeln/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

With 294 industrial robots per 10,000 employees, Switzerland was narrowly in the global top 10 in 2024, but well behind South Korea (1,220), Singapore (818), Germany (449) and Japan (446). Doubling to around 600 would put Switzerland ahead of Germany. Industry has employed a fairly stable 630,000 to 650,000 people since 2010, but its share of all employed persons is falling. Studies from comparable countries show clear productivity gains from robots; the effect on employment is mixed and depends on how the restructuring is handled.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

Robot density comes from the World Robotics Report 2025 of the International Federation of Robotics (IFR): installed industrial robots per 10,000 employees in manufacturing, as of 2024. According to the IFR, the figures for China are based on revised labour market data and are not comparable with earlier editions; for this reason we show no time series of robot density. Employment comes from the Swiss Labour Force Survey (SLFS) of the FSO, sections B–E (industry, mining, energy and water supply). Up to 2009 the figures are second-quarter values, from 2010 annual averages; the break is visible in the chart. We take the effects of robots from peer-reviewed studies on other countries; there is no comparable study for Switzerland.

---

### Switzerland in comparison

At 294, Switzerland is above the EU average (231) and the world average (132), but below countries with similarly high wage levels and strong export industries such as Germany, Japan, Sweden and Denmark. A target of around 600 (double the 2024 value) is ambitious but clearly below South Korea and Singapore. A high-wage country with a skills shortage, in particular, has a strong reason to automate production rather than relocate it.

---

### Industrial employment: stable in absolute terms

Between 1991 and 2004, the number of employed persons in sections B–E fell from around 798,000 to 634,000. Since then it has fluctuated within a narrow band; in 2025 it was 633,600. Industry has therefore not disappeared; for two decades it has held its employment steady in absolute terms.

---

### Industrial share: slowly declining

Because total employment grew (2025: 4.89 million employed persons), industry's share fell from 21.2% (1991) to 13.0% (2025). More automation need not accelerate this trend: where production stays in the country or returns thanks to robots, jobs in planning, maintenance, quality assurance and supply also stay.

---

### What research shows about robots, productivity and work

- **Productivity:** in 17 countries from 1993 to 2007, increased robot use contributed around 0.37 percentage points to annual labour productivity growth, raised total factor productivity and lowered product prices. Total employment did not fall significantly, but the share of low-skilled labour did (Graetz and Michaels, 2018).
- **Germany:** job losses in industry due to robots were fully offset by new jobs in the service sector. Existing employees more often stayed with the same firm and took on new tasks; those mainly affected were young labour-market entrants who never entered industry in the first place (Dauth et al., 2021).
- **USA:** one additional robot per 1,000 workers reduced the employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42% in heavily affected regions (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020).

The differences between Germany and the USA show that the labour market adapts better where firms retrain their people and redeploy them internally. These findings cannot be transferred one-to-one to Switzerland, but they show what matters.

---

## What this means for policy

- **A measurable target:** double robot density to around 600 by 2035 and report it annually on the basis of IFR data: [Reindustrialization with Robotics](@/robotik.en.md).
- **Targeted support for SMEs:** large exporters automate on their own. The leverage lies with SMEs, for example through shared test centres, leasing models and advisory services.
- **Organise the transition within firms:** the German pattern — retraining within the same firm instead of dismissal — should be supported with training vouchers and apprenticeship occupations in robotics and maintenance: [Work Without Fear](@/uebergaenge.en.md).

---

## Sources

1. International Federation of Robotics (IFR): Robot density surges in Europe, Asia and Americas (World Robotics 2025), 8 April 2026. https://ifr.org/ifr-press-releases/news/robot-density-surges-in-europe-asia-and-americas
2. Federal Statistical Office (FSO), SLFS: Erwerbstätige nach Wirtschaftsabschnitten [employed persons by economic section] (T 03.02.01.20), 1991–2025. https://www.bfs.admin.ch/asset/de/36494612
3. Graetz, G. and Michaels, G. (2018): Robots at Work. Review of Economics and Statistics 100(5), 753–768. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_00754
4. Dauth, W., Findeisen, S., Suedekum, J. and Woessner, N. (2021): The Adjustment of Labor Markets to Robots. Journal of the European Economic Association 19(6), 3104–3153. https://doi.org/10.1093/jeea/jvab012
5. Acemoglu, D. and Restrepo, P. (2020): Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets. Journal of Political Economy 128(6), 2188–2244. https://doi.org/10.1086/705716

---

# How Switzerland understands itself: English is more widespread in daily life than any second national language

> 44% of the population regularly use English, but only 15% of German-speaking Switzerland use French and 16% of French-speaking Switzerland use German. At work, English is growing fastest. At the same time, 86% consider several national languages important for cohesion.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/sprachen-verstaendigung-zahlen/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Switzerland is multilingual, but not in the way the picture of four national languages suggests. According to the Federal Statistical Office's (FSO) 2024 Survey on Language, Religion and Culture, 44% of the population aged 15 and over regularly use English. Far fewer use the other major national language: 15% of German-speaking Switzerland use French, 16% of French-speaking Switzerland use German. At work, 24% of employed people usually speak English, up from 17% in 2010. At the same time, 86% consider knowledge of several national languages important for the country's cohesion. The data show no either-or, but a gap between aspiration and everyday life.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

Figures on regularly used languages, language skills and attitudes come from the FSO's Survey on Language, Religion and Culture (ESRK) 2024: around 14,500 respondents aged 15 and over, surveyed from April to June 2024. "Regularly used" means spoken, written, read or heard at least once a week, at home, in leisure time, in the media or at work. The language region is determined by place of residence. The time series on main languages and languages at work come from the censuses (up to 2000) and the annual structural survey (from 2010). Since 2010, respondents can name up to three main languages; the jump in non-national languages between 2000 and 2010 is therefore largely methodological. In 2024 the ESRK was conducted mostly online for the first time, so we do not compare its values with the 2014 and 2019 waves. Information on school language teaching comes from the EDK, Eurydice and the Federal Council.

---

### English ahead of the second national language

In all three major language regions, more people regularly use English than any other national language: in German-speaking Switzerland 45.1% English versus 15.0% French; in French-speaking Switzerland 40.9% English versus 15.8% German (Swiss German: 6.5%); in Italian-speaking Switzerland 33.6% English versus 22.2% German and 18.6% French. Italian-speaking Switzerland is the region where the other national languages are most present in daily life.

---

### At work: English is growing fastest

From 2010 to 2024, the share of employed people who usually speak English at work rose from 16.5% to 23.6%. Swiss German fell from 67.2% to 60.8%, French from 29.2% to 27.6%; Standard German rose from 32.4% to 35.6%. According to the FSO, English grew most between 2014 and 2024 among 15- to 24-year-olds (from 14% to 22%) and is most widespread in companies with 500 or more full-time equivalents, at 27%. Even so, 95% of employed people speak at least one national language at work.

---

### Main languages: the population is becoming more multilingual

In 2024, German (or Swiss German) is the main language of 61.1% of the resident population, French of 22.6%, Italian of 7.8% and Romansh of 0.4%. French has grown from 18.4% in 1970 to over 22%, while Italian has declined from 11.0% to 7.8%. 24.5% name a non-national language as (one of) their main languages; English rose from 4.2% (2010) to 6.5% (2024). Because multiple answers have been possible since 2010, the shares do not add up to 100%.

---

### Skills, generations and barriers

- **Most people know English; the national languages less well:** Among 15- to 64-year-olds who know a language that is not their main language, 53.4% in German-speaking Switzerland rate their active English as good or very good, but only 13.2% their French. In French-speaking Switzerland the figures are 48.4% for English and 14.0% for German.
- **Young people are more multilingual:** 81% of 15- to 24-year-olds regularly use at least two languages, compared with 38% of people aged 65 and over. Almost two thirds of 15- to 24-year-olds rate their active English as good or very good, compared with 42% of 45- to 64-year-olds.
- **Aspiration remains high, slightly lower among the young:** 85.9% consider knowledge of several national languages important for cohesion (German-speaking Switzerland 84.3%, French-speaking 89.1%, Italian-speaking 93.7%). 77.3% think the first foreign language at school should be a national language; among 15- to 24-year-olds it is around two thirds, 20 percentage points fewer than among those aged 65 and over.
- **Language as an everyday barrier:** 12% of the population have no national language as their main language, 4 percentage points more than in 2010; English is the most common among them, at 21%. Of people whose main language is not the local language, 31.3% had language difficulties in dealing with the authorities, 26.3% with health professionals and 25.0% at work or when looking for a job. In French-speaking Switzerland the share for dealings with the authorities is markedly higher, at 40%, than in German-speaking Switzerland (27%).

---

### School: which foreign language first?

Under the cantons' 2004 language strategy and the HarmoS concordat, children learn two foreign languages in primary school: a national language and English. The cantons choose the order. According to Eurydice (as of December 2023), 14 cantons start with English and 12 with a second national language; those starting with a national language include all French- and Italian-speaking cantons and, under an agreement from 2004, Bern, Basel-Landschaft, Basel-Stadt, Solothurn, German-speaking Fribourg and Upper Valais, which start with French. Since 2025, several German-speaking cantonal parliaments have decided to teach French only at lower secondary level, including Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Zurich, according to SRF. On 12 June 2026 the Federal Council therefore opened a consultation on amending the Languages Act (deadline: 5 October 2026): option 1 enshrines the HarmoS model; option 2 requires a second national language to begin in primary school and continue to the end of lower secondary. If the cantons refrain from deviating decisions, the Federal Council does not intend to submit the bill to Parliament.

---

### What the data do not show

The surveys analysed do not measure how often people use machine translation or AI tools to communicate across language boundaries. Whether such tools complement or replace learning a second national language has not been studied for Switzerland. Nor are there nationally comparable measurements of the language level pupils actually reach at the end of compulsory schooling; the language skills in the ESRK are self-assessments.

---

## What this means for policy

- **Strengthen both instead of playing them off against each other:** English is already the most widespread bridge language in daily life and at work; at the same time, large majorities want the national languages. Policy should preserve the national languages and recognise English as an additional common lingua franca: [Language & Understanding](@/sprache-verstaendigung.en.md).
- **Multilingual authorities where it has an impact:** Almost a third of people without the local language as their main language face language barriers with the authorities. Key official information and online services should therefore also be available in English: [Open Government](@/offener-staat.en.md).
- **Measure instead of guessing:** Instead of arguing about the order of foreign languages, cantons and the Confederation should regularly assess the level reached in national languages and English at the end of schooling, and recognise language skills acquired at work and in further education: [Talent, Integration & Rule of Law](@/talent-integration.en.md).

---

## Sources

1. Federal Statistical Office (FSO): Sprachliche Praktiken in der Schweiz. Ergebnisse der Erhebung zur Sprache, Religion und Kultur 2024, Neuchâtel 2025 (FSO number 1368-2401). https://dam-api.bfs.admin.ch/hub/api/dam/assets/34788128/master
2. Federal Statistical Office (FSO): Sprachen bei der Arbeit, Neuchâtel 2026 (FSO number 1795-2600). https://dam-api.bfs.admin.ch/hub/api/dam/assets/36630116/master
3. Federal Statistical Office (FSO), structural survey: Languages usually spoken at work, 2010–2024 (su-d-01.08.01.03). https://dam-api.bfs.admin.ch/hub/api/dam/assets/36399471/master

# Talent & Migration: Are Qualifications Being Used — or Left Unused?

> 36% of third-country nationals work below their level of qualification. This is not an integration failure — it is a loss of value added.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/talent-ueberqualifikation/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

In 2024 Switzerland recorded net migration of +82,792 people.
Yet many qualifications remain unused: 36% of third-country nationals
work below their level (vs. 13% of Swiss nationals). According to our own rough estimate, this
means around CHF 3.6 billion in forgone wages per year.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

Population data: FSO Population and Households Statistics (2010–2024).
Migration data: FSO migration statistics (1991–2024).
Overqualification: FSO Structural Survey / SLFS (self-assessment + formal qualification),
supplemented by the OECD Indicators of Talent Attractiveness 2023.

The loss estimate is our own rough estimate: around 200,000 overqualified
immigrant workers × an assumed wage gap of around CHF 18,000 per year
≈ CHF 3.6 billion. Both values are assumptions, not published statistics;
the figure indicates an order of magnitude.

---

### Foreign population by permit type

The composition of the foreign population has shifted: settled residents (C permits) remain the majority, but since 2021 the number of residence-permit holders (B) in particular has grown — from 759,769 to 915,566 (2024). The chart shows the development of the resident stock — steady growth that reflects the Swiss economy's demand for labour.

---

### Net migration by origin

Net migration shows who arrives and who leaves. EU/EFTA citizens account for the bulk of immigration — driven by the free movement of persons. Third-country nationals arrive in smaller numbers but face the greatest integration hurdles in the recognition of professional qualifications.

---

### Overqualification rate by origin group

36% of third-country nationals work below their level of qualification — almost three times the rate among Swiss nationals (13%). This is not an integration failure on the part of those affected but a structural problem: recognition of diplomas, language barriers and protected-profession rules prevent people from being employed in line with their qualifications.

---

### Sectors with a high share of overqualification

In certain sectors a particularly large amount of talent remains unused: hospitality, cleaning and retail employ a particularly large number of overqualified people. This is a loss of value added in two senses — for those affected (lower wages) and for the economy (unused skills).

---

## Limitations

- Overqualification is based on self-assessment and formal recognition of diplomas
- Not all foreign diplomas are automatically equivalent (language barriers, protected professions)
- The estimate of economic loss is our own rough estimate with assumed values (number of people affected; the wage gap varies widely by sector)
- SLFS data are sample data with confidence intervals

---

## Data sources

- FSO: Population and Households Statistics (STATPOP)
- FSO: migration statistics (international migration)
- FSO: Structural Survey — employment by qualification and nationality
- OECD: Indicators of Talent Attractiveness 2023

---

# Talent Visas Compared: Singapore, Hong Kong, the United Kingdom and Switzerland

> Singapore, Hong Kong and the United Kingdom have dedicated routes for top talent: without a job offer or with a clear salary threshold, a decision in around four weeks, family included. Switzerland has only the general quota procedure.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/talentvisa-im-vergleich/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Singapore (ONE Pass), Hong Kong (Top Talent Pass Scheme) and the United Kingdom (Global Talent) have created dedicated admission routes for top talent. What they have in common: clear criteria instead of a case-by-case labour market test, a decision within around four to eight weeks, and family included. Switzerland has no such route; researchers and founders from third countries go through the same quota procedure as all qualified workers. The point here is a narrow, fast route for a few thousand people a year, not more general immigration.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

We compare criteria, processing times, family reunification and case numbers, in each case from the information published by the competent authorities: Ministry of Manpower (Singapore), Immigration Department and Labour and Welfare Bureau (Hong Kong), Home Office (United Kingdom), State Secretariat for Migration and Federal Council (Switzerland). The case numbers are not directly comparable: the Swiss quotas apply to all qualified workers from third countries, not only to top talent; for Hong Kong only cumulative figures are available. Two values are therefore marked as estimates.

---

### Criteria and family

- **Singapore, ONE Pass (since 2023):** fixed monthly salary of at least 30,000 Singapore dollars with an established company, or outstanding achievements in research, science, culture or sport. Valid for up to 5 years; changing jobs, working for several employers or running one's own company without a new application. Spouses can work with a Letter of Consent.
- **Hong Kong, Top Talent Pass (since end of 2022):** annual income of at least HK$2.5 million or a degree from a university on the official list of top universities (with or without work experience). No job offer required. Stay of 24 to 36 months, extension only with employment or one's own company. Spouses are allowed to work.
- **United Kingdom, Global Talent (since 2020):** endorsement by a specialist body in research, culture or digital technology, or a recognised prize. No job offer required. Up to 5 years per grant, settlement possible after 3 or 5 years; partners and children can accompany.
- **Switzerland, admission from third countries:** application by the employer, proof of priority for domestic workers, local and industry-standard pay and working conditions, qualification as a manager, specialist or qualified worker (Art. 20–23 AIG [Foreign Nationals and Integration Act]). For 2025 and 2026, 8,500 quota permits apply in each year (4,500 B, 4,000 L). Family reunification for B permit holders is subject to conditions (Art. 44 AIG).

---

### Processing time

Singapore states "within 4 weeks for most cases", Hong Kong "normally around 4 weeks" after a complete application. In the United Kingdom, endorsement takes 2 weeks (with a job, fellowship or funding) to 5 weeks (peer review), followed by the visa decision in around 3 weeks. In Switzerland, the SEM expects 6 to 8 weeks "as a rule" from a complete application, longer for complex cases. A target of ten working days would therefore be faster than all three models; it presupposes a simplified, standardised procedure.

---

### Case numbers

Singapore issued around 3,000 ONE Passes in 2024; at the end of 2025 there were around 8,500 holders. The United Kingdom granted 3,877 Global Talent visas to main applicants outside the country in 2024. Hong Kong had approved over 120,000 applications by the end of January 2026, on average (estimate) just over 38,000 per year. Switzerland used 74% of its third-country quotas in 2024 (estimated at around 6,300), and around 52% by the end of September 2025. The quotas are therefore not the bottleneck; for top talent it is rather the procedures and their duration.

---

### United Kingdom: stable demand, few refusals

The number of Global Talent visas (in 2019 and partly 2020 still its predecessor, Exceptional Talent) rose from 794 (2019) to 4,112 (2023) and has since been around 3,900 per year; in addition, around 2,800 dependants each year. Refusals at the visa stage are rare (2025: 26), because selection takes place at the endorsement stage. Hong Kong shows the other side: of around 40,200 people whose first visa expired by January 2026, only around 20,800 applied for an extension. Broad criteria generate many applications, but not automatically people who stay.

---

## What this means for policy

- **A dedicated talent visa outside the quotas:** narrow, verifiable criteria (salary threshold or endorsement by the ETH Domain, universities, SNSF, Innosuisse), a decision within ten working days, family included: [Talent, Integration & Rule of Law](@/talent-integration.en.md).
- **Start small and measurable:** an order of magnitude like the United Kingdom or Singapore (a few thousand per year), not like Hong Kong; an annual report on permits granted, retention and company formations.
- **Measure retention, not volume:** the Hong Kong example shows that extension rates are more meaningful than application numbers.

---

## Sources

1. Ministry of Manpower Singapore: ONE Pass, Eligibility, Key facts, Apply for a pass. https://www.mom.gov.sg/passes-and-permits/overseas-networks-expertise-pass
2. Ministry of Manpower: Written answer to PQ on statistics on issuance of ONE Pass, 4 February 2025. https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/parliament-questions-and-replies/2025/0204-written-answer-to-pq-on-statistics-on-issuance-and-management-of-one-pass
3. Ministry of Manpower: Written answer to PQ on effectiveness of ONE Pass, 5 August 2026. https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/parliament-questions-and-replies/2026/0805-written-answer-to-pq-on-effectiveness-of-overseas-networks
4. Immigration Department Hong Kong: Top Talent Pass Scheme. https://www.immd.gov.hk/eng/services/visas/TTPS.html
5. Labour and Welfare Bureau: Talent attraction, paper for the LegCo Panel on Manpower, 23 February 2026. https://www.legco.gov.hk/yr2026/english/panels/mp/papers/mp20260223cb1-165-5-e.pdf
6. GOV.UK: Global Talent visa. https://www.gov.uk/global-talent and https://www.gov.uk/global-talent-researcher-academic
7. Home Office: Immigration system statistics, Entry clearance visa outcomes (Vis_D02), year ending June 2026. https://www.gov.uk/government/statistical-data-sets/immigration-system-statistics-data-tables
8. Federal Council: Bundesrat legt unveränderte Drittstaatenkontingente für 2026 fest [Federal Council sets unchanged third-country quotas for 2026], 19 November 2025. https://www.admin.ch/de/newnsb/7HwBjdg5HpBA
9. SEM: FAQ Arbeit, Dauer des Bewilligungsverfahrens [FAQ on work: duration of the permit procedure]. https://www.sem.admin.ch/sem/de/home/themen/arbeit/faq.0010.html
10. Bundesgesetz über die Ausländerinnen und Ausländer und über die Integration (AIG) [Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration], SR 142.20. https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2007/758/de

# Transparent by Law: 20 Years of the Freedom of Information Principle in Figures

> Access requests to the federal administration have more than tripled since 2015. In 2025, however, full access was granted in only 39% of cases, and the number of statutory exemptions is growing.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/transparent-per-gesetz/ · Published: 2026-11-08 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Since 1 July 2006, documents of the federal administration have in principle been public, and since 1 November 2023 access has in principle been free of charge. Demand has risen sharply: in 2025 the federal authorities reported 2,145 processed access requests, almost four times as many as in 2015. At the same time, the share of requests with full access fell to 39%, and the Federal Council and Parliament have exempted 13 areas from the Act entirely. Sweden and Estonia show what openness as the norm looks like.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

The federal figures come from the activity reports of the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC), most recently the 33rd report 2025/2026 with the statistics on access requests under the Freedom of Information Act (BGÖ/FoIA) for calendar year 2025. The authorities report their cases themselves; the FDPIC points out that the workload is not recorded consistently. There are no comparable overall statistics for Sweden and Estonia; the comparison is therefore limited to the statutory rules. Cantonal laws and Parliament itself do not fall under the FoIA.

---

### Demand is growing

In the first (half) year, 2006, 95 requests were received; in 2015 there were 600, in 2024 a peak of 2,232 and in 2025 2,145 (2,086 new plus 59 carried over from the previous year). According to the FDPIC, the annual number has more than tripled in ten years. Fees are the exception: in 2025 the federal authorities charged a total of 7,601 francs.

---

### Less full access

The share of requests with full access was stable at around 50% from 2020 to 2024 and fell to 39% in 2025. Partial or deferred access rose to 25%, while complete refusals remained at around 10%. Cases where no official document existed (13%) and pending requests (9%) rose sharply. The FDPIC also observes that the FoIA is sometimes used for purposes unrelated to transparency.

---

### Mediation takes too long

Anyone who disagrees with an authority's decision can request mediation from the FDPIC; in 2025 there were 203 requests. The law provides 30 days for this. In 2018 and 2019 the FDPIC met this deadline in about half of cases, since 2022 only in around a quarter (2025: 24%); 36% took more than 100 days. When mediation does take place, it is often successful: 73% of sessions ended in agreement.

---

### Exemptions and comparison

- **Growing exemptions:** since 2006 the Federal Council and Parliament have inserted 13 exemptions in special legislation, and according to the FDPIC at least 11 more are planned, often for supervisory authorities.
- **Sweden:** the principle of public access has applied since the Freedom of the Press Ordinance of 1766 and is now enshrined in Chapter 2 of the Tryckfrihetsförordningen (1949:105) [Freedom of the Press Act], i.e. at constitutional level. Authorities must release records promptly ("skyndsamt"); exemptions are listed exhaustively in the Public Access to Information and Secrecy Act.
- **Estonia:** the Public Information Act requires authorities to maintain publicly accessible electronic document registers; requests must be answered within five working days and are in principle free of charge.

### Interests and terms of office

Members of the Federal Assembly must disclose their professional activities, mandates and advisory functions and, since December 2019, state whether a mandate is paid or unpaid (Art. 11 ParlA). The Parliamentary Services publish the register online. The amount of remuneration does not have to be disclosed. There are no term limits at federal level, but there are in some cantons: in the Grand Council of Basel-Stadt, a four-year break is required after 16 years; in the Landrat of Basel-Landschaft, members who have served four consecutive terms may not stand for the next one (§ 54 KV BL [cantonal constitution]).

---

## What this means for policy

- **Justify exemptions and give them a time limit:** every new exemption from the FoIA with a public justification and an expiry date; the existing 13 are reviewed: [Open Government](@/offener-staat.en.md).
- **Proactive rather than on request:** document registers on the Estonian model, so that documents do not have to be requested individually in the first place.
- **Meet deadlines:** resource the FDPIC so that the 30-day deadline is the rule again; measure it publicly every year.
- **Put a figure on interests:** disclose income from mandates in bands; examine term limits on the Basel model.

---

## Sources

1. FDPIC: 33. Tätigkeitsbericht 2025/2026 [33rd activity report], chapter on the freedom of information principle and statistics on access requests 2025. https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/dam/de/sd-web/ZgZZm5CLxIFF/33_T%C3%A4tigkeitsbericht%202025-2026%20DE_Web.pdf
2. FDPIC: 32. Tätigkeitsbericht 2024/2025 [32nd activity report] (free of charge since 1 November 2023). https://www.oeffentlichkeitsgesetz.ch/deutsch/files/2025/07/Taetigkeitsbericht-DE.pdf
3. Bundesgesetz über das Öffentlichkeitsprinzip der Verwaltung (BGÖ) [Federal Act on Freedom of Information in the Administration], SR 152.3. https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2006/355/de
4. Sveriges riksdag: Tryckfrihetsförordning (1949:105). https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/tryckfrihetsforordning-1949105_sfs-1949-105/
5. Regeringskansliet: Offentlighetsprincipen och sekretess, kortfattat om lagstiftningen. https://regeringen.se/contentassets/243fe724fd9a41218886261ff999fc2a/offentlighetsprincipen-och-sekretess--kortfattat-om-lagstiftningen
6. Riigi Teataja: Public Information Act (Avaliku teabe seadus). https://www.riigiteataja.ee/en/eli/ee/Riigikogu/act/514112013001/consolide
7. Kultuuriministeerium (Estonia): File a request for information. https://kulka.ee/public-information/file-a-request-for-information
8. Parliamentary Services: Offenlegungspflicht der Ratsmitglieder [disclosure obligation of members]. https://www.parlament.ch/de/%C3%BCber-das-parlament/parlamentsportraet/ratsmitglieder/rechtsstellung-der-ratsmitglieder/offenlegungspflicht
9. Grosser Rat Basel-Stadt: Broschüre 2025. https://grosserrat.bs.ch/images/dateien/broschuere/2025_broschuere.pdf
10. Verfassung des Kantons Basel-Landschaft [Constitution of the Canton of Basel-Landschaft], SGS 100, § 54. https://bl.clex.ch/data/100

# Defence: What Does the Swiss Defence Franc Buy?

> According to SIPRI, Switzerland spent 0.76% of GDP on defence in 2025, less than any of the European countries compared. The question is not only how much more, but what for.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/verteidigung-ausgaben-prioritaeten/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

According to SIPRI, Switzerland spent 0.76% of GDP on defence in 2025
(USD 7.6 billion), after 0.70% in 2024. That puts it below all the
European countries compared. The militia army with around 140,000 members
keeps per-capita costs low, so the question is not only "how much more"
but "what for".

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

Defence expenditure as a share of GDP: SIPRI Military Expenditure Database
(April 2026 edition, 2000–2025, 7 countries). Cost per soldier: IISS
Military Balance 2024 (2023/24 data).

---

### Swiss spending trend

Swiss defence expenditure fell from around 1% of GDP (2000) to 0.64% (2014) and has since risen to 0.76% (2025), still well below 1% of GDP. In real terms it grew by 9.4% in 2025 compared with the previous year (SIPRI). The current political pressure to increase it contrasts with a decades-long trend of cuts — the question is not only "how much more" but "for what".

---

### International comparison

In international comparison, Switzerland is at the lower end: in 2025 Austria spent 1.1%, France 2.0%, Germany 2.3%, Sweden 2.5% and Finland 2.6% of GDP. At the summit in The Hague (June 2025), NATO members committed to spending 5% of GDP annually by 2035: at least 3.5% on core defence requirements and up to 1.5% on defence- and security-related spending such as infrastructure protection and resilience. This target does not apply to neutral Switzerland, and without alliance obligations the direct comparison is relative. The capability gaps, however, do not become any smaller.

---

### Cost per active soldier

The militia system leads to a particular cost structure: Switzerland has around 140,000 members of the armed forces, most of whom serve in the militia. Per-capita costs are therefore much lower than in professional armies. The figures are not directly comparable, because militia members do not fill full-time positions.

---

## Limitations

- Militia troop strength ≠ full-time equivalents (cost per member of the armed forces not directly comparable)
- Cost-per-soldier comparison based on IISS 2023/24 data, not updated
- SIPRI data: definitions of defence expenditure differ between countries; 2025 GDP shares based on IMF estimates

---

## Data sources

- SIPRI Military Expenditure Database, April 2026 edition: https://www.sipri.org/databases/milex (data table: https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/SIPRI-Milex-data-1949-2025.xlsx)
- SIPRI Fact Sheet "Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2025" (April 2026): https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/2604_milex_2025.pdf
- NATO: The Hague Summit, 24–25 June 2025 (5% of GDP by 2035, of which 3.5% core defence and 1.5% defence- and security-related spending), https://www.nato.int/en/news-and-events/articles/news/2025/06/27/nato-concludes-historic-summit-in-the-hague
- IISS: Military Balance 2024 — troop strength and budgets

---

# Continuing Education: Who Takes Part — and Who Does Not?

> The gap in continuing education is huge: highly qualified people take part 2.6× more often than those with low qualifications. Industries with a lot of manual work train the least — not the office occupations with the highest AI risk.

Source: https://die-zukunft.ch/en/zukunftslabor/notizen/weiterbildung-teilnahme-luecken/ · Published: 2026-02-12 · Publisher: The Future (Swiss political party, Basel)

Participation in continuing education is stagnating at 60% — and the gap between
highly and low-qualified people (79% vs. 30%) is enormous. The lowest rates are found in
hospitality, transport and construction — not in the industries with the highest AI risk.

<!-- more -->

---

## Methodology

Continuing education data from the FSO Microcensus on Education and Training
(2011, 2016, 2021). Participation in non-formal education (courses,
seminars, in-company training). Employment data from the FSO SLFS
(2024). Automation risk: modelled post-LLM industry values from the note
on automation risk by industry (our own assumptions based on the IMF,
Cazzaniga et al. 2024, not measured values).

---

### By level of education

Highly qualified people take part in continuing education 2.6 times more often than those with low qualifications. This gap is the central problem: those who are already well educated keep investing — those who need it most are left behind. Without targeted offerings for people with low qualifications, continuing education widens inequality instead of reducing it.

---

### By age group

Participation declines with age and drops markedly from 55 (55–64: 51%). Yet continuing education is crucial precisely for the 45–64 age group: they still have to hold their own for 15–20 years in a changing labour market. The decline is less an individual problem than a failure of the in-company and institutional provision.

---

### Time series

A decade of near standstill: the overall rate has hovered around 60% since 2011. Despite the debate on digitalisation, fears of automation and political rhetoric, actual participation in continuing education has changed little.

---

### Cross-analysis with automation risk

The relationship is weakly positive (r = 0.28): the industries with the highest post-LLM risk — finance, professional services, ICT — train above average (75–78%). The lowest rates are in hospitality (35%), other business services (38%) and transport (40%), whose risk lies in the middle range. That is where adaptability for the next structural change is missing — a structural risk that calls for targeted provision.

---

## Limitations

- The FSO Microcensus is conducted only every 5 years
- Industry-specific continuing education rates partly estimated
- Automation risk by industry is modelled, not measured
- Quality of continuing education not recorded (participation only)
- Correlation ≠ causation

---

## Data sources

- FSO: Mikrozensus Aus- und Weiterbildung [Microcensus on Education and Training] 2011, 2016, 2021
- FSO: SLFS 2024 — employed persons by economic section
- IMF: AI Preparedness Index 2024 (Cazzaniga et al.)
